Management Needs Answered: 
• Which cities/channels should get more investment? 
• Which products are actually profitable vs just high-volume? 
• How to optimize sales team performance and commission structure?

Help RetailMax optimize operations and boost profitability using Excel analytics!

Apply Conditional Formatting: 
1. Highlight profit margins >25% in GREEN 
2. Highlight profit margins <15% in RED 
3. Add data bars to Total_Sales column 
 
Create Reference Tables: Create a separate area with: 
• Sales Rep Commission Table:  
o Sales <₹50,000 = 2% commission 
o Sales ≥₹50,000 = 3% commission 
• Use VLOOKUP to add commission amount for each transaction 
 
 
TASK 2: Pivot Table Analysis  
1. Sales by City and Channel  
o Rows: City, Channel 
o Values: Sum of Total_Sales, Count of Transaction_ID 
o Add calculated field for Total Profit 
2. Monthly Performance  
o Rows: Month (group dates by month) 
o Columns: Category 
o Values: Sum of Total_Sales 
3. Product Category Analysis  
o Rows: Category, Product_Name 
o Values: Sum of Total_Sales, Sum of Quantity 
o Filter by City 
4. Customer Type Analysis  
o Rows: Customer_Type, Payment_Method 
o Values: Average of Total_Sales, Count of transactions 
 
 
 
TASK 3: Dashboard Creation  
Create a Business Dashboard including: 
1. Top 5 performing cities (use formulas) 
2. Best-selling product categories (from pivot data) 
3. Monthly sales trend chart 
 
 
Deliverables: 
1. Complete Excel File with all sheets properly formatted 
2. Business Insights Summary (in a text box or separate sheet) 
3. What recommendations would you give for Q1 2025 strategy? 
4. Top 3 Strategic Recommendations based on your analysis

title: Case Study on Supply Chain Optimization – Retail
question:
• How does the shift from a centralized distribution model to a multi-echelon 
network impact overall transportation and warehousing costs? 
• What are the key data points required to build a highly accurate, predictive 
demand forecasting model for retail? 
• How can a retailer handle sudden shifts in consumer demand that historical 
data might fail to predict (e.g., unexpected viral trends)? 
• What are the operational risks of relying too heavily on automated replenishment 
systems without human oversight?
solution_approach:
Case Study on Supply Chain Optimization – Retail 
5. How a large retail chain redesigned its supply chain to balance inventory, reduce 
stockouts, and improve demand forecasting. 
Introduction A large retail chain operating over 200 stores faced significant logistical 
challenges, struggling to maintain appropriate stock levels across its network. The 
company experienced frequent stockouts of fast-moving consumer goods alongside an 
accumulation of slow-moving excess inventory. This case study analyzes the supply 
chain optimization strategies used to redesign their distribution model and balance 
inventory. 
Background Before the optimization effort, the retailer relied heavily on a rigid, 
centralized distribution model and rudimentary demand forecasting methods. This 
setup caused long lead times for store replenishment. The inability to accurately predict 
local store demand resulted in a severe mismatch of inventory levels, frustrating 
customers with empty shelves for popular items while tying up capital in stagnant 
regional warehouse stock. 
Optimization Strategies 
• Predictive Demand Forecasting: The retailer leveraged historical sales data, 
local seasonal trends, and external variables (such as local events or weather) 
using machine learning algorithms. This shifted forecasting from a regional 
aggregate to highly accurate, localized predictions at the individual store level. 
• Hub-and-Spoke Distribution Redesign: The company transitioned from a 
strictly centralized model to a multi-echelon "hub-and-spoke" network. They 
introduced smaller, localized fulfillment centers closer to high-density store 
clusters to drastically reduce replenishment lead times. 
• Automated Replenishment and Min/Max Levers: Dynamic Min/Max inventory 
levers driven by real-time Point of Sale (POS) data were implemented. This 
system triggered automatic reordering for fast-moving items just in time, 
preventing stockouts without over-ordering. 
• SKU Rationalization and Redistribution: By analyzing inventory turnover ratios, 
the supply chain team identified slow-moving products (SKUs). They initiated 
targeted markdowns and dynamically redistributed excess stock from regional 
warehouses to specific stores where localized demand for those specific items 
was higher. 
 
 
Impact 
• Reduced Stockouts: Real-time data integration and localized forecasting 
drastically decreased the out-of-stock rate for high-velocity items, directly 
increasing top-line revenue and customer trust. 
• Optimized Inventory Capital: Redistributing and rationalizing slow-moving 
items freed up valuable working capital and reduced warehousing holding costs. 
• Shortened Lead Times: The decentralized, multi-echelon distribution network 
allowed for agile, and in some cases same-day, replenishment for critical stock. 
• Enhanced Customer Satisfaction: Consistent product availability improved the 
overall shopping experience, driving repeat foot traffic and brand loyalty. 
Final Note The retailer's turnaround highlights the critical shift from a push-based, 
centralized supply chain to a pull-based, data-driven network. By leveraging advanced 
analytics for forecasting and decentralizing distribution, the company successfully 
aligned its inventory levels with actual consumer demand, transforming a logistical 
liability into a competitive advantage. 
Questions for Discussion 
• How does the shift from a centralized distribution model to a multi-echelon 
network impact overall transportation and warehousing costs? 
• What are the key data points required to build a highly accurate, predictive 
demand forecasting model for retail? 
• How can a retailer handle sudden shifts in consumer demand that historical 
data might fail to predict (e.g., unexpected viral trends)? 
• What are the operational risks of relying too heavily on automated replenishment 
systems without human oversight?

title: Case Study on M&A Due Diligence – Telecom
question:
• Why might a target company in the telecom sector intentionally defer 
infrastructure maintenance prior to seeking an acquisition? 
• How does discovering significant "technical debt" during due diligence directly 
impact the final valuation and negotiation strategy of a deal? 
• What steps can an acquiring company take to protect itself if it discovers minor 
regulatory non-compliance during the final stages of due diligence? 
• How should the acquiring company balance the urgency to close a competitive 
deal with the thoroughness required for a comprehensive due diligence process?
solution_approach:
Case Study on M&A Due Diligence – Telecom 
6. How a national telecom company conducted comprehensive due diligence to 
evaluate the acquisition of a regional ISP and mitigate hidden risks. 
Introduction A leading national telecom company sought to rapidly expand its 
broadband footprint and customer base by evaluating the acquisition of a regional 
Internet Service Provider (ISP). While the target company presented highly attractive 
financial metrics on the surface, the acquirer needed to validate the deal's true value. 
This case study details the due diligence approach utilized to uncover hidden liabilities, 
assess regulatory compliance, and validate infrastructure quality. 
Background The telecommunications sector is highly capital-intensive and heavily 
regulated. Prior to initiating formal due diligence, the national telecom company noted 
that the regional ISP's reported profit margins were unusually high compared to industry 
benchmarks. This raised initial concerns regarding potential underinvestment in 
network maintenance, hidden operational liabilities, and regulatory compliance gaps 
that could jeopardize the acquisition's long-term viability. 
Due Diligence Approach & Red Flags 
• Technical and Infrastructure Assessment: The company deployed network 
engineers to audit the quality, age, and capacity of the physical broadband 
infrastructure (e.g., fiber versus legacy copper wiring). Red flags targeted: 
Deferred maintenance, outdated hardware nearing end-of-life, or a lack of 
scalability to support future bandwidth demands. 
• Quality of Earnings (QoE) Analysis: Financial experts conducted a deep dive to 
normalize EBITDA and verify the sustainability of revenue streams. Red flags 
targeted: Premature revenue recognition, high customer churn rates masked by 
aggressive short-term promotional discounting, or massive off-balance-sheet 
liabilities. 
• Regulatory and Legal Compliance Audit: Legal teams reviewed local municipal 
agreements, right-of-way access rights, and spectrum licenses. Red flags 
targeted: Pending litigation, expiring local permits, or non-compliance with data 
privacy regulations. 
• Customer and Contract Diligence: The team reviewed the terms of enterprise 
contracts and analyzed the retail customer base for satisfaction and retention 
metrics. Red flags targeted: A high concentration of revenue tied to a few easily 
terminable enterprise contracts, or a history of frequent network outages leading 
to poor customer reviews. 
 
Impact 
• Risk Mitigation: The multi-pronged due diligence approach successfully 
identified areas where the regional ISP had deferred maintenance, allowing the 
acquirer to forecast and prepare for necessary capital expenditures post-merger. 
• Valuation Adjustment: By uncovering hidden operational liabilities and the true 
cost of upgrading legacy hardware (technical debt), the national telecom 
company was able to negotiate a fairer, reduced purchase price. 
• Regulatory Assurance: Confirming the validity of local licenses and right-of-way 
agreements ensured that expansion plans would not be halted by legal 
injunctions post-acquisition. 
• Strategic Integration Planning: A clear understanding of the target's operational 
state allowed the national telecom to build a realistic timeline, roadmap, and 
budget for integrating the regional infrastructure into its national network. 
Final Note This case underscores that surface-level financials are insufficient for 
validating high-stakes M&A transactions, particularly in asset-heavy industries like 
telecommunications. A rigorous, cross-functional due diligence approach—spanning 
financial, technical, and legal domains—is essential to uncover red flags, accurately 
value the target, and ensure the strategic goals of the acquisition are safely met. 
Questions for Discussion 
• Why might a target company in the telecom sector intentionally defer 
infrastructure maintenance prior to seeking an acquisition? 
• How does discovering significant "technical debt" during due diligence directly 
impact the final valuation and negotiation strategy of a deal? 
• What steps can an acquiring company take to protect itself if it discovers minor 
regulatory non-compliance during the final stages of due diligence? 
• How should the acquiring company balance the urgency to close a competitive 
deal with the thoroughness required for a comprehensive due diligence process?

financial metrics on the surface, the acquirer needed to validate the deal's true value. 
This case study details the due diligence approach utilized to uncover hidden liabilities, 
assess regulatory compliance, and validate infrastructure quality. 
Background The telecommunications sector is highly capital-intensive and heavily 
regulated. Prior to initiating formal due diligence, the national telecom company noted 
that the regional ISP's reported profit margins were unusually high compared to industry 
benchmarks. This raised initial concerns regarding potential underinvestment in 
network maintenance, hidden operational liabilities, and regulatory compliance gaps 
that could jeopardize the acquisition's long-term viability. 
Due Diligence Approach & Red Flags 
• Technical and Infrastructure Assessment: The company deployed network 
engineers to audit the quality, age, and capacity of the physical broadband 
infrastructure (e.g., fiber versus legacy copper wiring). Red flags targeted: 
Deferred maintenance, outdated hardware nearing end-of-life, or a lack of 
scalability to support future bandwidth demands. 
• Quality of Earnings (QoE) Analysis: Financial experts conducted a deep dive to 
normalize EBITDA and verify the sustainability of revenue streams. Red flags 
targeted: Premature revenue recognition, high customer churn rates masked by 
aggressive short-term promotional discounting, or massive off-balance-sheet 
liabilities. 
• Regulatory and Legal Compliance Audit: Legal teams reviewed local municipal 
agreements, right-of-way access rights, and spectrum licenses. Red flags 
targeted: Pending litigation, expiring local permits, or non-compliance with data 
privacy regulations. 
• Customer and Contract Diligence: The team reviewed the terms of enterprise 
contracts and analyzed the retail customer base for satisfaction and retention 
metrics. Red flags targeted: A high concentration of revenue tied to a few easily 
terminable enterprise contracts, or a history of frequent network outages leading 
to poor customer reviews. 
 
Impact 
• Risk Mitigation: The multi-pronged due diligence approach successfully 
identified areas where the regional ISP had deferred maintenance, allowing the 
acquirer to forecast and prepare for necessary capital expenditures post-merger. 
• Valuation Adjustment: By uncovering hidden operational liabilities and the true 
cost of upgrading legacy hardware (technical debt), the national telecom 
company was able to negotiate a fairer, reduced purchase price. 
• Regulatory Assurance: Confirming the validity of local licenses and right-of-way 
agreements ensured that expansion plans would not be halted by legal 
injunctions post-acquisition. 
• Strategic Integration Planning: A clear understanding of the target's operational 
state allowed the national telecom to build a realistic timeline, roadmap, and 
budget for integrating the regional infrastructure into its national network. 
Final Note This case underscores that surface-level financials are insufficient for 
validating high-stakes M&A transactions, particularly in asset-heavy industries like 
telecommunications. A rigorous, cross-functional due diligence approach—spanning 
financial, technical, and legal domains—is essential to uncover red flags, accurately 
value the target, and ensure the strategic goals of the acquisition are safely met. 
Questions for Discussion 
• Why might a target company in the telecom sector intentionally defer 
infrastructure maintenance prior to seeking an acquisition? 
• How does discovering significant "technical debt" during due diligence directly 
impact the final valuation and negotiation strategy of a deal? 
• What steps can an acquiring company take to protect itself if it discovers minor 
regulatory non-compliance during the final stages of due diligence? 
• How should the acquiring company balance the urgency to close a competitive 
deal with the thoroughness required for a comprehensive due diligence process?

title: CASE STUDY #6 – DIGITAL
question:
● What would a realistic forcing function for ONDC look like, and should government try to 
manufacture one via regulation rather than relying on organic adoption? 
● Is Namma Yatri evidence that ONDC works, or evidence that a well-executed, commission-free app 
succeeded largely independent of ONDC's interoperability premise? 
● As ONDC's CEO, would you double down on all verticals, focus on 1–2, or wind down the operating 
company and open-source the protocol?
solution_approach:
CASE STUDY #6 — DIGITAL 
Can ONDC Beat Amazon/Flipkart/Swiggy-Zomato? 
Data current as of July 2026. Sources: ONDC/PIB materials, NPCI/UPI statistics, CCI investigation 
coverage. 
Introduction 
UPI succeeded because it solved a real, painful, single problem — fragmented payment rails — at the right 
regulatory moment. Does ONDC have an equivalent forcing function, or is it a solution without a clear killer use 
case? 
Background 
ONDC is not a shopping app — it is a set of open, government-incubated protocol specifications (built on the 
Beckn Protocol) letting independent buyer apps, seller apps, and logistics providers transact with each other, the 
same conceptual move UPI made for payments. It was incorporated as a Section 8 non-profit in December 2021 
under DPIIT and launched publicly in April 2022, conceived as a structural remedy to CCI's antitrust concerns 
about Amazon and Flipkart's 25–40% platform commissions. 
As of April 2025, ONDC had onboarded ~7.6 lakh sellers across 600+ cities, but the rigorous picture is weaker: 
retail orders peaked at 6.5 million/month in Oct 2024 then fell ~35% once subsidies were cut, only 1.16 lakh 
sellers were actually "live" as of December 2025 versus 700,000+ onboa rded, and FY25 posted a net loss of 
₹147.13 crore on revenue of just ₹33.41 crore. Amazon and Flipkart still command ~83% of Indian e -
commerce, while quick commerce is the real growth frontier. 
Approach: Three Scenarios for How ONDC Could Gain Share 
● Scenario 1 — Vertical Focus: concentrate on one or two categories with genuine traction (mobility, 
per the Namma Yatri success story) or structural cost advantage (hyperlocal kirana grocery), mirroring 
UPI's own playbook of winning one problem before expanding. Plausibility: medium-high. 
● Scenario 2 — Digital Public Utility for Underserved Segments: reposition ONDC as infrastructure 
for segments private platforms underserve — rural producers, transit ticketing, sachetized financial 
products — rather than a head-on Amazon/Flipkart challenger. Plausibility: medium. 
● Scenario 3 — Protocol Devolution: ONDC exits its operating role; the Beckn Protocol moves to an 
independent body for neutral governance, while government shifts to standard -setting and regulation 
instead of subsidies. Plausibility: medium-low near-term, but the most coherent long-run fix. 
Key Structural Challenges Observed 
● Trust & grievance redressal: across multi-party transactions, "who do I call when my order is wrong?" 
has no clean answer the way it does on a vertically integrated platform. 
● Buyer-app concentration and exit risk: demand depends on a handful of VC -funded apps whose own 
economics drive participation, as PhonePe's Pincode exit demonstrated. 
● Governance conflicts: DigiHaat is simultaneously a network participant and a competitor to the private 
buyer apps ONDC needs to court. 
● A market that moved on: quick commerce's dark-store model has become the real growth frontier, one 
a pure interoperability protocol can't easily replicate. 
Final Note 
The UPI comparison mostly shows why commerce is structurally harder than payments, not why ONDC should 
follow a similar timeline. Four years of weak retail traction likely reflects both a timing problem (network 
effects in commerce take longer) and a design problem (breadth-over-depth strategy, governance conflicts, 
unstable protocol tooling) that money alone will not fix. 
Questions for Discussion 
● What would a realistic forcing function for ONDC look like, and should government try to 
manufacture one via regulation rather than relying on organic adoption? 
● Is Namma Yatri evidence that ONDC works, or evidence that a well-executed, commission-free app 
succeeded largely independent of ONDC's interoperability premise? 
● As ONDC's CEO, would you double down on all verticals, focus on 1–2, or wind down the operating 
company and open-source the protocol?

title: CASE STUDY #10 – DIGITAL
question:
● What demand proxy would you use to pick which tier-2 cities to enter first? 
● How would you design a store's break-even timeline so leadership knows when to shut down an 
underperforming store versus giving it more ramp time? 
● Does quick commerce's cost structure ever work in lower-density tier-2 markets, or does the model 
require a different format there?
solution_approach:
CASE STUDY #10 — DIGITAL 
Quick Commerce's Dark Store Expansion Dilemma 
Introduction 
Quick commerce players (Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart) have proven that 10-minute delivery is possible in dense 
metro clusters by pre-positioning inventory in small, hyperlocal "dark stores." A challenger player must decide 
whether to expand aggressively into tier-2 cities now to claim first-mover share, or consolidate density in 
existing metros first. 
Background 
The dark-store model inverts traditional e-commerce economics: a dense grid of 1,500–3,000 sq. ft. micro-
fulfilment stores stocks 2,000–5,000 SKUs within a 2 km delivery radius, enabling 10–15 minute delivery. A 
store needs roughly 300–400 daily orders to break even, but a new store in an unproven market may start at only 
40–60 orders per day and take 6–12 months to ramp. Metro markets are increasingly saturated, while tier-2 
cities are underserved but come with lower order density, higher per-order delivery costs, and less proven rental 
economics. 
Approach: Strategic Options Evaluated 
● Option A — Aggressive Tier-2 Land Grab: expand rapidly into 15–20 tier-2 cities over 12 months to 
capture prime real estate and brand recall before rivals, at the risk of burning cash on stores below 
break-even density. 
● Option B — Metro Density Consolidation First: pause new-city expansion, add infill stores in 
existing metros, and delay tier-2 entry by 12–18 months, improving near-term unit economics but 
ceding first-mover positioning. 
● Option C — Selective, Data-Led Tier-2 Pilots: enter only 3–5 tier-2 cities with strong digital-grocery 
penetration as instrumented pilots, scaling the playbook only to cities that hit density targets within 4 –6 
months. 
Recommended Path & Expected Impact 
● Option C balances first-mover advantage with capital discipline, generating real data before 
committing further capital at scale. 
● The value of prime dark-store real estate is partly a scarce, first-mover asset, which argues against 
waiting too long (Option B alone). 
● A disciplined pilot approach preserves the option to scale fast into any tier-2 city that proves out, while 
avoiding a multi-city cash burn if the model doesn't translate. 
Final Note 
The right answer blends unit economics (orders-per-store-per-day versus break-even threshold) with real-
options thinking: small, instrumented pilots preserve the option to scale or exit cheaply, which is why a 
disciplined middle path between all-in expansion and full consolidation is usually the strongest 
recommendation. 
Questions for Discussion 
● What demand proxy would you use to pick which tier-2 cities to enter first? 
● How would you design a store's break-even timeline so leadership knows when to shut down an 
underperforming store versus giving it more ramp time? 
● Does quick commerce's cost structure ever work in lower-density tier-2 markets, or does the model 
require a different format there?

disciplined middle path between all-in expansion and full consolidation is usually the strongest 
recommendation. 
Questions for Discussion 
● What demand proxy would you use to pick which tier-2 cities to enter first? 
● How would you design a store's break-even timeline so leadership knows when to shut down an 
underperforming store versus giving it more ramp time? 
● Does quick commerce's cost structure ever work in lower-density tier-2 markets, or does the model 
require a different format there?

title: CASE STUDY #12 – DIGITAL
question:
● Why can a blended metric like overall conversion rate mask a channel-mix problem, and how should 
reporting be redesigned to avoid this? 
● What are the risks of introducing a lower-priced micro-offer specifically for low-intent users? 
● How should the client balance cheap-but-low-intent acquisition channels against more expensive but 
higher-converting ones?
solution_approach:
CASE STUDY #12 — DIGITAL 
EdTech Freemium-to-Premium Conversion Decline 
Introduction 
The client operates a freemium test-prep app with 5 million monthly active free users and a premium 
subscription tier priced at ₹999/month. Over the past two quarters, the free-to-paid conversion rate has fallen 
from 3.2% to 1.6%, even as free-user signups continued to grow. 
Background 
Marketing spend on acquisition has stayed flat, and the premium feature set has not changed. Management 
wants a root-cause diagnosis and a plan to restore conversion. 
Approach: Step-by-Step Diagnostic Walkthrough 
● Step 1 — Break Down Conversion: Conversion = (Users who hit a paywall) × (Paywall-to-trial rate) 
× (Trial-to-paid rate). Isolate which stage of the chain has degraded. 
● Step 2 — Analyze Paywall Exposure: the share of free users who ever encounter a paywall has 
actually risen, so exposure is not the problem. 
● Step 3 — Analyze Paywall-to-Trial Rate: this rate has fallen sharply — fewer users who see the 
paywall are starting a free trial, even though trial length and terms are unchanged.  
● Step 4 — Segment the Drop: the decline is concentrated among users acquired through referral and 
short-video ads, which now account for 55% of new signups, versus organic and search where rates are 
stable. 
● Step 5 — Identify the Root Cause: users from referral and short-video channels arrive with lower 
intent — drawn by viral content or referral incentives rather than an active exam-prep need — so they 
structurally convert at a lower rate. The acquisition mix shift, not a product or pricing change, is 
diluting blended conversion. 
Root Cause and Recommended Actions 
● Root Cause: a shift in acquisition mix toward lower-intent channels (referral, short-video ads) is 
dragging down blended conversion, not a weaker product or paywall experience.  
● Short-Term: report conversion by acquisition channel rather than blended, and introduce a lighter-
weight, lower-price micro-offer for low-intent channel users. 
● Long-Term: rebalance acquisition spend toward higher-intent channels, and build an intent-scoring 
model at signup to route users into differentiated onboarding and monetization funnels. 
Final Note 
Fixing the measurement first — segmenting conversion by channel — and the funnel second, with a 
differentiated offer for low-intent users, addresses the actual driver of the decline rather than making product or 
pricing changes aimed at the whole user base. 
Questions for Discussion 
● Why can a blended metric like overall conversion rate mask a channel-mix problem, and how should 
reporting be redesigned to avoid this? 
● What are the risks of introducing a lower-priced micro-offer specifically for low-intent users? 
● How should the client balance cheap-but-low-intent acquisition channels against more expensive but 
higher-converting ones?

question: Analyze the following business challenge: Consulting Case Study. Outline your structured approach, root cause diagnosis, and recommendations.
solution_approach:
Consulting Case Study  
Digital Fleet Optimization & Predictive 
Maintenance Transformation for a 
Logistics Company  
Executive Summary (TL;DR) 
SwiftMove Logistics, a fictional logistics company operating 4,800 trucks across India, 
experienced rising fuel costs, poor vehicle utilization, unexpected breakdowns, and declining on-
time deliveries. A consulting engagement redesigned fleet planning, maintenance, and route 
optimization using digital technologies. Within 12 months, on-time delivery improved from 84% 
to 96%, fuel costs fell by 14%, fleet utilization increased by 18%, and maintenance expenses 
dropped by 21%. 
1. Background 
Rapid expansion left fleet operations decentralized. Regional managers scheduled maintenance 
independently, routes were manually planned, and GPS data was underutilized. Customer 
complaints increased as delivery delays became more frequent. 
2. Business Challenge 
Executive leadership asked consultants to: 
• Reduce transportation costs without expanding the fleet. 
• Improve delivery reliability and customer satisfaction. 
• Build a scalable operating model using digital technologies. 
3. Consulting Methodology 
• Phase 1 – Fleet Diagnostic: Assess vehicle utilization, maintenance history, fuel consumption 
and delivery performance. 
• Phase 2 – Route Analytics: Identify inefficient routes using GPS and traffic data. 
• Phase 3 – Maintenance Redesign: Introduce predictive maintenance based on vehicle health 
data. 
• Phase 4 – Digital Platform Integration: Integrate fleet management, warehouse and 
customer tracking systems. 
• Phase 5 – Pilot Rollout: Implement solutions in two logistics hubs. 
• Phase 6 – Enterprise Scale-up: Expand nationwide with governance dashboards. 
4. Key Considerations 
• Vehicle breakdowns caused 37% of delivery delays. 
• Fuel consumption differed significantly across similar routes. 
• Maintenance schedules were time-based instead of condition-based. 
• Customers lacked real-time shipment visibility. 
5. Sample Deliverables 
Deliverable Business Value 
Fleet Performance Dashboard Monitor operational KPIs 
Predictive Maintenance Framework Reduce unexpected failures 
Route Optimization Report Lower fuel and transit costs 
Transformation Roadmap Guide phased implementation 
6. Strategic Recommendations 
• Deploy AI-enabled route optimization. 
• Adopt predictive maintenance using IoT vehicle sensors. 
• Create a centralized Fleet Operations Control Center. 
• Provide customers with live shipment tracking. 
• Standardize KPIs across all regional hubs. 
7. Technology & Change Management 
Implement an integrated Transportation Management System (TMS), GPS analytics platform, 
and predictive maintenance engine. Train dispatchers, maintenance teams, and drivers through 
phased workshops while linking performance incentives to operational KPIs. 
8. Risk Identification 
Risk Impact Mitigation 
Driver resistance Medium Training & incentive 
programs 
Poor GPS data quality High Data validation framework 
Technology integration 
delays 
High Phased implementation 
Supplier downtime Medium Backup maintenance 
partners 
 
9. Cost–Benefit Analysis 
Transformation investment: ₹26 Crore. 
Annual business benefit: ₹48 Crore through fuel savings, reduced maintenance, improved fleet 
utilization, and lower customer penalties. 
Estimated payback period: 8–10 months. 
10. Monitoring KPIs 
• On-time Delivery: 84% → 96% 
• Fuel Cost: -14% 
• Fleet Utilization: +18% 
• Maintenance Cost: -21% 
• Vehicle Breakdown Rate: -38% 
• Customer Satisfaction: +22% 
11. Future Operating Model & ROI 
A Fleet Transformation Office was established to oversee route optimization, predictive 
maintenance, KPI governance, and continuous improvement. Cross-functional collaboration 
between operations, IT, procurement, and customer service ensured sustainable operational 
excellence. 
12. Key Findings & FAQs 
Q: What was the primary cause of delays? 
A: Unplanned vehicle breakdowns and inefficient routing. 
 
Q: Which initiative generated the highest ROI? 
A: Predictive maintenance combined with AI-based route optimization. 
 
Q: How was long-term success sustained? 
A: Central governance, digital dashboards, standardized KPIs, and continuous analytics.

title: CASE STUDY #1 – TELECOM
question:
● In the absence of a competitor benchmark, how should a company decide between pricing aggressively 
for share versus pricing high for margin? 
● What risks does the client take on by being the first mover in setting the market's 5G price anchor?  
● How should the tiered pricing structure evolve once the competitor eventually announces its own 5G 
tariffs?
solution_approach:
CASE STUDY #1 — TELECOM 
5G Commercial Tariff Pricing Strategy 
Introduction 
The client is one of the largest telecom operators in India, with a pan-India presence and an extensive 4G 
subscriber base. It has recently completed a significant phase of its 5G infrastructure rollout across more than 
500 cities, but has not yet introduced a dedicated commercial 5G tariff plan. 
With increasing investments in spectrum acquisition, network infrastructure, and operational capabilities, 
management wants to determine an appropriate pricing strategy before the nationwide commercial launch of 5G  
plans. 
Background 
The Indian telecom market is largely a duopoly. The client's primary competitor has also expanded its 5G 
network to more than 450 cities but has not yet announced dedicated 5G plans, leaving the market without 
established pricing benchmarks. 
The client must arrive at a price for its first 5G data + unlimited voice plan while simultaneously balancing 
customer adoption, profitability, and long-term market positioning — with no direct precedent to anchor against. 
Approach: Hybrid Pricing Strategy (Cost-Based + Value-Based) 
The client adopted a hybrid pricing approach, using value-based pricing as the primary method and cost-based 
pricing as a validation floor. 
● Cost-Based Pricing (validation floor): determine the minimum sustainable price by factoring in 
spectrum costs, infrastructure, operations, maintenance, marketing spend, and a target profit margin. 
This ensures recovery of 5G investment but does not reflect what customers are actually willing to pay.  
● Value-Based Pricing (primary method): determine the final market price based on the incremental 
value 5G delivers — higher speeds, lower latency, improved reliability, and richer digital services. 
With no competitor benchmark available, this is the most defensible pricing lens.  
● Tiered Launch Pricing: launch affordable, tiered 5G plans in the ₹499–₹1,299/month range to lower 
the adoption barrier for the mass 4G base while still segmenting for heavier users.  
Expected Impact 
● Encourages rapid migration of the existing 4G base onto 5G, accelerating network monetization. 
● Improves ARPU progressively as customers move up the tiered plan structure over time.  
● Recovers 5G infrastructure investment through volume-led adoption rather than relying on high initial 
tariffs that could suppress uptake. 
● Establishes the client as the price-setter in a market with no existing 5G tariff benchmark, shaping 
competitor response. 
Final Note 
By anchoring price to customer-perceived value rather than cost alone, and validating that price against a 
sustainable cost floor, the client can launch 5G tariffs that drive adoption without leaving money on the table — 
a critical balance in a market entering commercial 5G pricing for the first time. 
Questions for Discussion 
● In the absence of a competitor benchmark, how should a company decide between pricing aggressively 
for share versus pricing high for margin? 
● What risks does the client take on by being the first mover in setting the market's 5G price anchor?  
● How should the tiered pricing structure evolve once the competitor eventually announces its own 5G 
tariffs?

title: Digital Transformation Strategy in Specialty
question:
Where does the current digital estate create or 
destroy value? Which capability gaps most constrain growth and competitiveness? 
Phase 2 — Strategic Opportunity Mapping & Prioritization 
Cross-functional workshops surface candidate use cases across R&D, commercial, and manufacturing. Each is 
scored on strategic value and feasibility to produce a prioritized digital opportunity portfolio, rather than a wish 
list of disconnected pilots. 
Phase 3 — Target Operating Model & Roadmap Design 
With priorities set, the team designs the target operating model — governance bodies, decision rights, funding 
mechanisms, and talent model — needed to sustain delivery, and sequences initiatives into a multi-year 
roadmap. 
Phase 4 — Technology & Data Architecture Design 
This phase defines the reference architecture: a unified cloud data platform, master data management standards, 
and interoperability protocols (including healthcare data standards such as HL7 FHIR) that allow the prioritized 
use cases to be built on common foundations rather than one-off integrations. 
Phase 5 — Pilot Execution and Scaling 
Selected initiatives are piloted in controlled scope, validated against predefined success metrics, and then 
scaled deliberately — avoiding both premature scaling of unproven concepts and indefinite pilot purgatory. 
Phase 6 — Governance, Talent, and Continuous Improvement 
The final phase embeds an operating rhythm — steering committee cadence, KPI reviews, and talent 
development — that allows the digital portfolio to evolve as market conditions, regulation, and technology 
continue to change. 
3. Key Considerations for the Board 
The Board will likely ask how the strategy avoids becoming another wave of disconnected pilots. The answer 
lies in the prioritization discipline of Phase 2 and the operating model established in Phase 3: initiatives are 
funded and governed as a portfolio, not approved individually based on whichever function advocates most 
persuasively. 
A second likely concern is pace: pharmaceutical organizations operate under regulatory constraints that can 
slow technology adoption relative to other industries. The roadmap is deliberately structured with regulatory 
and compliance review built into each stage gate, rather than treated as a final hurdle after solutions are built. 
The Board will also want clarity on return on investment. Upfront investment in shared data infrastructure is 
significant, but the long-term benefit is that each subsequent use case is built faster and at lower marginal cost 
— the economics improve as the portfolio matures. 
Expected business outcomes: 
• Faster, more consistent commercial engagement across HCP and patient channels 
• Reduced cycle time from data collection to R&D and real-world-evidence insight 
• Improved manufacturing responsiveness to demand volatility 
Potential implementation challenges: 
• Resistance to change from functions accustomed to independent technology budgets 
• Data privacy and security requirements across multiple jurisdictions 
• Legacy system dependencies that complicate near-term integration 
Relevant Critical Success Factors and KPIs: 
• Time-to-insight for R&D and real-world evidence generation 
• Commercial cost-to-serve per HCP / patient interaction 
• Percentage of digital initiatives meeting stage-gate value targets 
• Data platform adoption rate across business functions 
4. Sample Deliverables 
• Digital Opportunity Prioritization Matrix (Excel) 
• Digital Transformation Roadmap (PowerPoint) 
• Target Operating Model Blueprint (PowerPoint / Word) 
• Business Case & Value Tracking Model (Excel) 
• Data Governance & Interoperability Playbook (PDF) 
• Digital KPI Dashboard Template (Excel) 
5. Strategic Alignment with Corporate Strategy 
Digital transformation is not pursued as a standalone initiative; it must be explicitly linked to the corporate 
growth strategy — whether that strategy emphasizes specialty pipeline expansion, geographic growth, or 
margin improvement ahead of anticipated biosimilar competition. Each element of the digital roadmap is 
mapped back to the corporate strategic priority it advances, which keeps prioritization decisions grounded in 
enterprise value rather than functional preference. 
6. Culture and Change Leadership 
Digital transformation in a historically siloed organization succeeds or fails on leadership behavior. Executives 
across R&D, commercial, and manufacturing must visibly sponsor cross-functional initiatives and be willing to 
reallocate budget and talent away from legacy, function-specific systems. Incentive structures are adjusted so 
that functional leaders are rewarded for enterprise outcomes — such as faster time-to-insight — rather than for 
the size of their independent technology budget. 
7. Technology and Data Architecture Enablement 
A unified cloud data platform and common data model are the foundation on which prioritized use cases are 
built — from AI-assisted real-world evidence generation in R&D, to next-best-action engagement models in 
commercial, to predictive demand sensing in manufacturing. Interoperability standards, including healthcare-
specific protocols such as HL7 FHIR, ensure that data generated in one function can be trusted and reused by 
another, rather than re-collected and reconciled department by department. 
8. Regulatory and Compliance Landscape 
Data privacy and clinical data-handling requirements (including HIPAA, GDPR, and evolving FDA guidance 
on AI-enabled tools) shape both the pace and the architecture of the transformation. Rather than treating 
compliance as a constraint to be managed at the end of each project, the strategy embeds regulatory and 
privacy review at each stage gate — turning disciplined compliance into a source of competitive advantage and 
trust with regulators, physicians, and patients, rather than a source of delay. 
9. Opportunity Identification and Prioritization 
Opportunity identification combines structured workshops across R&D, medical affairs, commercial, and 
manufacturing with a quantitative scoring model that weighs strategic value, feasibility, and time-to-value. This 
produces a two-by-two prioritization view that distinguishes quick wins from foundational, longer-horizon 
investments — for example, a next-best-action commercial engagement tool might score high on both value 
and near-term feasibility, while an enterprise real-world-evidence platform scores high on value but requires 
the shared data architecture to be in place first. 
10. Cost-Benefit Analysis and Business Case Development 
Each initiative in the portfolio carries its own business case, weighing upfront technology and change-
management investment against quantifiable benefits — commercial revenue uplift, R&D cycle-time 
reduction, and manufacturing cost avoidance — as well as harder-to-quantify benefits such as regulatory

have been pursued opportunistically, without a shared view of which capabilities create the greatest strategic 
value. A second hypothesis is that the operating model — governance, talent, and incentives — has not evolved 
to support cross-functional digital initiatives, leaving high-potential pilots stranded before they scale. A third 
possibility is that the organization lacks the data architecture and interoperability standards required to convert 
existing technology investment into usable, trusted insight.

A six-phase approach is proposed to move the organization from fragmented technology spend to a coherent 
digital transformation strategy. 
Phase 1 — Digital & Data Diagnostic 
The engagement opens with a comprehensive diagnostic of the existing technology estate, data flows, and 
digital capability maturity relative to peers. Key questions: Where does the current digital estate create or 
destroy value? Which capability gaps most constrain growth and competitiveness? 
Phase 2 — Strategic Opportunity Mapping & Prioritization 
Cross-functional workshops surface candidate use cases across R&D, commercial, and manufacturing. Each is 
scored on strategic value and feasibility to produce a prioritized digital opportunity portfolio, rather than a wish 
list of disconnected pilots. 
Phase 3 — Target Operating Model & Roadmap Design 
With priorities set, the team designs the target operating model — governance bodies, decision rights, funding 
mechanisms, and talent model — needed to sustain delivery, and sequences initiatives into a multi-year 
roadmap.

and interoperability protocols (including healthcare data standards such as HL7 FHIR) that allow the prioritized

Selected initiatives are piloted in controlled scope, validated against predefined success metrics, and then 
scaled deliberately — avoiding both premature scaling of unproven concepts and indefinite pilot purgatory. 
Phase 6 — Governance, Talent, and Continuous Improvement 
The final phase embeds an operating rhythm — steering committee cadence, KPI reviews, and talent 
development — that allows the digital portfolio to evolve as market conditions, regulation, and technology 
continue to change.

slow technology adoption relative to other industries. The roadmap is deliberately structured with regulatory

significant, but the long-term benefit is that each subsequent use case is built faster and at lower marginal cost

Digital transformation is not pursued as a standalone initiative; it must be explicitly linked to the corporate 
growth strategy — whether that strategy emphasizes specialty pipeline expansion, geographic growth, or 
margin improvement ahead of anticipated biosimilar competition. Each element of the digital roadmap is 
mapped back to the corporate strategic priority it advances, which keeps prioritization decisions grounded in 
enterprise value rather than functional preference.

title: CASE STUDY #2 – TELECOM
question:
● Why is it important to trace a financial symptom (declining profit) all the way down to an operational 
root cause (ringing duration) rather than stopping at the cost-line explanation? 
● What are the risks of unilaterally shortening ringing duration without a regulatory standard in place?  
● How could the client have detected this issue earlier, before seven months of profitability erosion?
solution_approach:
CASE STUDY #2 — TELECOM 
Profitability Decline — Root-Cause Diagnosis 
Introduction 
The client is one of the largest pan-India telecom operators. Over the past seven months, it has experienced a 
significant decline in profitability while competitors reported increasing profits over the same period.  
Background 
The client operates as a pure-play telecom service provider, offering voice, data, broadband, and other telecom 
services. Management wants to identify the root cause of the declining profitability and recommend practical 
solutions that improve financial performance without compromising customer experience. 
Approach: Step-by-Step Diagnostic Walkthrough 
● Step 1 — Analyze Profitability: break down Profit = Revenue − Cost, to determine whether the 
decline stems from reduced revenue or increased costs. 
● Step 2 — Analyze Revenue: review major revenue streams — voice/SMS/internet, broadband & 
DTH, OTT/data partnerships, and net network exchange fee — to isolate the area of concern, which 
turns out to be the Net Network Exchange Fee. 
● Step 3 — Analyze Network Exchange Fee: split the fee into receipts from other operators versus 
payments to other operators; the rise in payments made is what is driving the profitability decline.  
● Step 4 — Identify the Cause: network exchange payments depend on the number of outgoing calls, 
call duration, and per-minute charges; the key finding is a rise in outgoing calls, driven mainly by an 
increase in callback calls. 
● Step 5 — Identify the Root Cause: map the customer call journey (Dial → Ring → Wait → 
Connect); competitors reduced their ringing duration from 45 seconds to 25 seconds, causing more 
missed calls on the client's network and, consequently, more callback calls — raising inter-network 
traffic and network exchange payments. 
Root Cause and Recommended Actions 
● Root Cause: higher network exchange payments resulting from increased callback calls, driven by 
competitors' shorter ringing duration. 
● Short-Term: match competitors' ringing duration, and engage with TRAI to address the issue and seek 
regulatory support. 
● Long-Term: negotiate better inter-network usage agreements with competitors, and work with TRAI 
to standardize call ringing duration across the industry. 
Final Note 
Reducing callback traffic by aligning ringing duration with competitors, combined with regulatory intervention, 
addresses the immediate profitability drain. Longer term, renegotiated inter-network agreements and an 
industry-wide ringing-duration standard would remove the structural cost disadvantage altogether.  
Questions for Discussion 
● Why is it important to trace a financial symptom (declining profit) all the way down to an operational 
root cause (ringing duration) rather than stopping at the cost-line explanation? 
● What are the risks of unilaterally shortening ringing duration without a regulatory standard in place?  
● How could the client have detected this issue earlier, before seven months of profitability erosion?

CASE STUDY #4 — TELECOM 
MobiWave's Postpaid Billing Nightmare 
Billing Transformation & Customer Churn 
Introduction 
MobiWave, a regional telecom operator, launched a new bundled postpaid plan combining mobile data, home 
broadband, and OTT streaming subscriptions. Within weeks, the company's churn rate spiked from 2% to 6% 
monthly. 
Background 
Customer care was overwhelmed with billing disputes — customers were being charged incorrectly for bundles, 
some were double-billed for OTT add-ons, and others couldn't get their loyalty discounts applied. The issue 
traced back to gaps in MobiWave's BSS architecture: the product catalog wasn't updated to define the new 
bundle as a single rateable product, the mediation layer was dropping or duplicating usage records, CRM was 
not synced with billing, and revenue-assurance reconciliation was a manual weekly batch process rather than 
continuous monitoring. 
Approach: BSS Concepts Applied 
BSS Function Issue Identified Fix Implemented 
Product Catalog / Order 
Management 
New bundle not modeled correctly 
as one product 
Redesigned catalog with bundle-
level rating rules 
Mediation & Rating Usage data duplication/loss across 
sources 
Implemented unified mediation layer 
with deduplication logic 
Convergent Billing Fragmented billing across services Migrated to a single convergent 
billing engine 
CRM Integration Care agents lacked real-time billing 
visibility 
Integrated CRM with billing via 
APIs for a single customer view 
Revenue Assurance Manual, delayed reconciliation Automated real-time reconciliation 
with exception alerts 
Self-Care Channels Outdated bill representation Synced self-care app with new 
billing engine 
Resolution & Outcome 
MobiWave rebuilt its product catalog for accurate bundle rating, deployed a unified mediation and convergent 
billing platform, and integrated CRM with billing for a single customer view. Within two months: 
● Billing-related complaints dropped by 60% 
● Monthly churn returned to 2.3% 
● Revenue leakage from billing errors reduced by an estimated 15% 
Final Note 
The billing nightmare was a product-modeling problem before it was a technology problem: treating a genuinely 
bundled offer as three disconnected line items broke every downstream system that touched it. Fixing the 
catalog at the source resolved the churn and complaint spike.

question:
● If you were advising the DoT, would you convert more debt to equity again if Vi asks in 2027 –28? 
● Is a government-controlled Vodafone Idea good or bad for Indian consumers? 
● Vi has ruled out 5G FWA while Jio and Airtel race into it — good focus, or a category it can't afford to 
cede? 
● How would you judge whether the AGR relief actually "worked"? What FY27 –29 metrics would you 
track?
solution_approach:
CASE STUDY #5 — TELECOM 
Vodafone Idea's Survival in a Duopoly Market 
Data current as of July 2026. Sources: TRAI, company results, analyst notes. 
Introduction 
The Indian government has converted a large chunk of Vodafone Idea's (Vi) AGR and spectrum dues into 
equity, becoming its largest shareholder at 48.99%. Is this a genuine survival path, or a slow -motion 
nationalization / managed exit? Against Jio and Airtel's tariff, network, and capex dominance, the question is 
what Vi should actually do differently. 
Background 
As of April 2026 TRAI data, Reliance Jio holds 39.25% market share (499.3 million subscribers, ₹214 ARPU), 
Bharti Airtel holds 37.81% (480.9 million subscribers, ₹257 ARPU), Vodafone Idea holds 15.61% (198.5 
million subscribers, ₹190 ARPU), and BSNL holds 7.31% (93.0 million subscribers). Jio and Airtel together 
hold ~77% of subscribers, and Vi's share has been on a multi-year secular decline, though net additions turned 
marginally positive by Q1 FY27. 
Vi's balance sheet crisis traces back to the 2019–2020 Supreme Court AGR ruling, a 2021–2023 payment 
moratorium with ~₹16,000 crore of interest converted to equity (making government a ~33% shareholder) , an 
April 2025 conversion of ₹36,950 crore of spectrum dues (pushing the government stake to 48.99%), and a Dec 
2025–Apr 2026 DoT reassessment cutting Vi's AGR liability from ₹87,695 crore to ₹64,046 crore with 
repayment pushed to FY32–FY41. 
The core structural problem is capex: Jio and Airtel together invested ₹1.3–1.7 trillion in network expansion 
during FY21–FY25, while Vi's cumulative capex over the same period was only ~₹22,500 crore — roughly 6–
8% of what its rivals spent during the exact years 5G was rolled out nationally. 
Approach: Strategic Options Considered 
● Option A — Aggressive Capital Catch-Up: raise substantially more capital to fund a much larger 
capex program targeting 5G and enterprise parity in Vi's 17 priority circles. The only path that 
plausibly regains share, but requires capital multiples beyond what has been raised and deepens 
nationalization optics. 
● Option B — Capex-Light Differentiation: concentrate on the 17 priority circles, skip capital-
intensive FWA, lean on the AST SpaceMobile satcom partnership for rural coverage, and push tariff 
hikes toward the industry's ₹300 ARPU aspiration. Matches spending to Vi's actual balance sheet, but 
analysts expect it to only stabilize share near 16%, not grow it. 
● Option C — Accept Managed Decline: treat Vi as a wind-down/consolidation candidate — harvest 
cash from the core, avoid further large capex, and prepare for eventual formal restructuring or sale. 
Financially honest given the capex math, but politically costly given 193 million subscribers a nd 
banking exposure. 
Strategic Implications 
● Competitive strategy: in network industries, capex is the primary moat — coverage drives retention, 
which drives ARPU, which funds further capex. Vi is caught in reverse of this cycle.  
● Unit economics: Vi's ARPU (₹190) trails Airtel (₹257) and Jio (₹214); much of its survival case rides 
an industry-wide tariff tailwind it doesn't have to fight for, but the capex it needs to fund alone.  
● Political economy: with government simultaneously regulator, creditor, and major ity shareholder, a 
"correct" pure corporate-strategy answer (e.g., harvest cash) can be right for Vi as a company while 
politically unacceptable for its majority owner. 
● The strongest reading is that Option B is already the de facto strategy, with the real question being how 
much of Option A's capital scale can realistically be layered onto it before promoters or government 
balk, and Option C as the implicit fallback. 
Final Note 
The government has floor-priced Vi's downside risk without fixing its structural capex deficit. Vi's survival is no 
longer purely a market outcome — it is a managed, state-influenced equilibrium, and any strategic 
recommendation has to be evaluated against both corporate and political-economy constraints simultaneously. 
Questions for Discussion 
● If you were advising the DoT, would you convert more debt to equity again if Vi asks in 2027 –28? 
● Is a government-controlled Vodafone Idea good or bad for Indian consumers? 
● Vi has ruled out 5G FWA while Jio and Airtel race into it — good focus, or a category it can't afford to 
cede? 
● How would you judge whether the AGR relief actually "worked"? What FY27 –29 metrics would you 
track?

question:
● How should the client structure sales incentives differently for enterprise deals versus its existing 
consumer sales motion? 
● What capabilities does the operator need to build in-house versus partner for (e.g., systems integrators 
for private networks)? 
● How can the client defend this enterprise revenue once competitors replicate the same use -case 
roadmap?
solution_approach:
CASE STUDY #7 — TELECOM 
5G Enterprise B2B Monetization Strategy 
Introduction 
The client is a leading pan-India telecom operator that has completed its 5G rollout across 500+ cities. 
Consumer 5G adoption is growing, but ARPU gains have plateaued because rivals offer near -identical consumer 
plans. 
Background 
Management believes the larger untapped opportunity lies in enterprise (B2B) 5G use cases — private networks, 
network slicing, and IoT connectivity — but the client has no established enterprise go-to-market motion and 
limited experience selling to industrial customers. The CFO wants a monetization roadmap before competitors 
capture large anchor accounts. 
Approach: Use-Case Prioritization Framework 
Enterprise 5G use cases were prioritized on two axes: revenue potential (deal size, recurring revenue, cross -sell) 
and feasibility (technical readiness, sales-cycle length, capital intensity). 
● Manufacturing Private 5G Networks: high revenue potential and moderate feasibility — factories 
need low-latency, secure connectivity for robotics and AGVs, but sales cycles run 9 –12 months. 
● Smart Logistics & Fleet IoT: high feasibility, moderate revenue — leverages existing IoT SIM 
infrastructure and sells faster, though with smaller deal sizes. 
● Healthcare Remote Diagnostics: high revenue potential, low near-term feasibility — requires ultra-
reliable low-latency slicing and regulatory clearance. 
● Smart City / Utility Grids: government-anchored, moderate revenue, long procurement cycles — 
valuable for reference customers rather than near-term revenue. 
Recommended Rollout & Expected Impact 
● Horizon 1 (0–12 months): monetize smart logistics and fleet IoT using existing infrastructure to 
generate quick, referenceable wins. 
● Horizon 2 (12–24 months): build a dedicated enterprise sales pod and land 3–5 anchor manufacturing 
private-network deals to prove the model. 
● Horizon 3 (24+ months): scale into healthcare and smart-city verticals once network-slicing SLAs and 
regulatory pathways mature. 
Final Note 
Sequencing the roadmap this way converts 5G capex into enterprise revenue faster than a simultaneous multi -
vertical push, since each horizon's reference customers de-risk the next. 
Questions for Discussion 
● How should the client structure sales incentives differently for enterprise deals versus its existing 
consumer sales motion? 
● What capabilities does the operator need to build in-house versus partner for (e.g., systems integrators 
for private networks)? 
● How can the client defend this enterprise revenue once competitors replicate the same use -case 
roadmap?

title: CASE STUDY #8 – TELECOM
question:
● Why can a network appear "fully covered" on paper while still failing customers at the exact mome nts 
that matter most? 
● What are the trade-offs of triggering capacity upgrades on peak-hour utilization versus average 
utilization? 
● How should SignalNet prioritize investment between the top 20 revenue circles and its broader network 
footprint going forward?
solution_approach:
CASE STUDY #8 — TELECOM 
SignalNet's Urban Network Congestion Crisis 
Capacity Planning & Network Operations 
Introduction 
SignalNet, a metro-focused operator with 12 million subscribers, saw data speeds collapse during peak hours 
(7–10 PM) across its top 20 revenue-generating cities, even though the operator's headline network-coverage 
maps showed "full 4G/5G availability." 
Background 
Customers reported buffering on video calls and app timeouts. Churn in the affected circles rose from 1.8% to 
4.1% monthly within one quarter, concentrated among high-ARPU postpaid users. Investigation revealed that 
cell-site capacity upgrades were triggered by average utilization rather than peak-hour utilization, the network 
had no dynamic load-balancing between overlapping 4G and 5G layers, KPI dashboards reported city -wide 
averages that masked hyper-local congestion, and network performance data was never linked to customer 
complaint or churn data. 
Approach: OSS Concepts Applied 
OSS Function Issue Identified Fix Implemented 
Capacity Management Upgrades triggered on average, not 
peak, utilization 
Shifted trigger thresholds to 95th-
percentile peak-hour utilization 
Traffic Engineering / SON No dynamic load balancing across 
4G/5G layers 
Deployed Self-Organizing Network 
(SON) load-balancing between 
carriers 
Performance Management (FCAPS) City-level KPI averaging hid local 
hotspots 
Introduced grid-level (500m) 
congestion heatmaps 
Customer Experience Management No link between network KPIs and 
churn/complaints 
Built a CEM layer correlating cell-
level performance with complaint 
and churn data 
Site Planning / Rollout New site approvals were slow and 
reactive 
Adopted a rolling 90-day proactive 
densification plan for top-20 revenue 
circles 
Resolution & Outcome 
Within one quarter of implementing the changes: 
● Peak-hour data speeds in the top 20 circles improved by 38% 
● Postpaid churn in affected circles fell from 4.1% back to 2.0% 
● Congestion-related complaint volume dropped by 42% 
Final Note 
The crisis was rooted in a measurement blind spot, not a raw capacity shortfall: averaged KPIs hid the peak -
hour, hyper-local congestion that customers actually experienced. Fixing what engineering measured — and 
linking it to churn — fixed the underlying problem. 
Questions for Discussion 
● Why can a network appear "fully covered" on paper while still failing customers at the exact mome nts 
that matter most? 
● What are the trade-offs of triggering capacity upgrades on peak-hour utilization versus average 
utilization? 
● How should SignalNet prioritize investment between the top 20 revenue circles and its broader network 
footprint going forward?

CASE STUDY #9 — TELECOM 
Stalled Prepaid-to-Postpaid Migration 
Introduction 
The client, a pan-India telecom operator, derives 92% of its subscriber base from prepaid, well above the 
industry's postpaid mix. Postpaid customers carry roughly 3x the ARPU and are stickier, so management 
launched a campaign to migrate high-usage prepaid customers to postpaid plans. 
Background 
After six months, migration volumes are less than 15% of target, despite eligible customers being offered a free 
trial month and a discounted postpaid tariff. Management wants a root-cause diagnosis of why migration is 
stalling. 
Approach: Step-by-Step Diagnostic Walkthrough 
● Step 1 — Define the Funnel: break the migration journey into Eligible → Offered → Interested → 
Enrolled, and measure drop-off at each stage rather than looking only at the final conversion number. 
● Step 2 — Locate the Drop-Off: 78% of eligible customers were offered the plan and 61% expressed 
interest, but only 16% of interested customers actually enrolled — the funnel breaks late, at enrollment. 
● Step 3 — Investigate the Enrollment Stage: postpaid enrollment requires in-store KYC re-
verification and a security deposit, while prepaid customers are used to instant, app -based top-ups with 
zero paperwork. 
● Step 4 — Segment the Drop-Off: drop-off is heavily concentrated among customers in tier-2/3 cities, 
where the nearest company-owned store averages 9 km away, versus tier-1 cities where drop-off is far 
lower. 
● Step 5 — Identify the Root Cause: the migration offer is well-targeted and well-received, but the in-
store KYC enrollment channel imposes a physical-access cost that a purely digital prepaid customer 
base is not willing to absorb. 
Root Cause and Recommended Actions 
● Root Cause: enrollment requires physical store visits for KYC re-verification, creating an access 
barrier for a digital-first customer base located far from company-owned stores. 
● Short-Term: enable Video KYC and Aadhaar e-KYC for postpaid enrollment, and waive the security 
deposit for customers with 12+ months of clean prepaid payment history.  
● Long-Term: build a hybrid "postpaid-lite" product with prepaid-style instant top-up UX but postpaid 
billing, and expand doorstep KYC agent networks in tier-2/3 cities. 
Final Note 
Digitizing the KYC and enrollment journey end-to-end matches the frictionless UX prepaid customers already 
expect from the brand, addressing the actual bottleneck rather than further discounting an offer customers 
already find attractive. 
Questions for Discussion 
● Why is it important to measure drop-off at each funnel stage rather than just the overall conversion 
rate? 
● What risks does waiving the security deposit based on prepaid payment history introduce, and how 
should they be managed? 
● How might the postpaid-lite hybrid product cannibalize the client's existing prepaid or postpaid 
revenue?

question:
1. Why is the CRM platform not being fully adopted by employees?  
2. Which business functions are most affected by poor CRM adoption?  
3. What are the possible reasons for declining sales productivity and customer satisfaction?  
4. What recommendations would you provide to improve CRM adoption and business 
performance?  
5. Prepare a roadmap to achieve 90% CRM adoption within the next 12 months.  
 
Candidate Instructions 
You have 25–30 minutes to analyze the case and present your recommendations. 
While solving the case: 
 Identify the key business problem.  
 State any assumptions made.  
 Select an appropriate framework.  
 Analyze the available information.  
 Prioritize recommendations.  
 Present a structured solution to the CEO.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Solution 
Q1. Why is the CRM platform not being fully adopted by 
employees? 
The CRM implementation challenge is primarily driven by people and process issues rather 
than technology. Employees continue using familiar tools like spreadsheets and emails because 
of limited training, resistance to change, and the absence of standardized CRM usage across 
departments. 
Key Reasons 
Issue Impact 
Resistance to change Employees continue manual processes 
Inadequate training Low confidence in CRM usage 
Lack of standard processes Inconsistent data entry 
No leadership monitoring Low accountability 
Conclusion: The CRM system is available, but user adoption remains low due to poor change 
management. 
 
Q2. Which business functions are most 
affected by poor CRM adoption? 
Business Function Impact 
Sales Poor pipeline visibility and lower lead conversion 
Marketing Difficulty measuring campaign effectiveness 
Customer Success Delayed customer issue resolution 
Management Inaccurate reporting and forecasting 
Conclusion: Poor CRM adoption affects decision-making across the organization. 
 
Q3. What are the possible reasons for 
declining sales productivity and customer 
satisfaction? 
Sales Productivity 
 Incomplete customer information  
 Manual lead tracking  
 Longer sales cycle  
 Poor collaboration between teams  
Customer Satisfaction 
 Slow response time  
 Delayed issue resolution  
 Inconsistent customer communication  
 Lack of complete customer history  
Observation: Low CRM adoption directly impacts both sales efficiency and customer 
experience. 
 
Q4. What recommendations would you 
provide to improve CRM adoption and 
business performance? 
Focus Area Recommendation 
People Conduct CRM training and awareness sessions 
Process Standardize CRM usage across departments 
Technology Simplify workflows and improve system usability 
Governance Monitor CRM usage through KPIs and leadership reviews 
Expected Outcome: Higher CRM adoption, improved collaboration, and better customer 
management. 
 
Q5. Prepare a roadmap to achieve 90% CRM 
adoption within the next 12 months. 
Timeline Key Actions Expected Outcome 
0–3 
Months 
Employee training, define CRM guidelines, 
identify CRM champions 
Increase awareness and initial 
adoption 
3–6 
Months 
Standardize sales and customer support 
processes, monitor CRM usage Improve process compliance 
6–12 
Months 
Introduce dashboards, performance tracking, 
and incentives for CRM adoption 
Achieve 90% adoption and 
improved business performance 
 
Final Recommendation 
TechNova should focus on people, processes, and governance rather than changing the CRM 
platform. By improving employee adoption, standardizing business processes, and continuously 
monitoring CRM usage, the company can enhance sales productivity, customer satisfaction, and 
maximize the return on its CRM investment.

2. Which business functions should management prioritize for improvement?  
3. What are the possible reasons for declining customer satisfaction and increasing 
employee attrition?  
4. What recommendations would you provide to improve operational efficiency and 
profitability?  
5. Prepare a strategic roadmap that helps NexGen improve its EBITDA margin over the 
next three years.  
 
Candidate Instructions 
You have 25–30 minutes to analyze the case and present your recommendations. 
While solving the case: 
 Clearly define the problem statement.  
 State any assumptions made.  
 Choose an appropriate consulting framework.  
 Analyze the available information logically.  
 Prioritize recommendations based on business impact.  
 Summarize your final recommendations to the CEO. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Q1. Why is the company's profitability 
declining despite increasing revenues? 
Although NexGen's revenue has increased consistently, its EBITDA margin has declined from 
16% to 11%. This indicates that operating costs are growing faster than revenue. 
Key Reasons 
Issue Business Impact 
High employee attrition Increased hiring and training costs 
Low employee utilization Higher operational costs 
Declining customer satisfaction Lower client retention and repeat business 
Low lead conversion Reduced sales efficiency 
Project delays Increased delivery costs and customer dissatisfaction 
Conclusion: Profitability is declining mainly due to operational inefficiencies rather than lack 
of revenue growth. 
 
Q2. Which business functions should 
management prioritize for improvement? 
Business Function Priority 
Human Resources Reduce attrition and improve retention 
Project Delivery Improve execution and resource utilization 
Sales & Business Development Increase lead conversion 
Customer Success Improve customer satisfaction and retention 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Q3. What are the possible reasons for 
declining customer satisfaction and 
increasing employee attrition? 
Customer Satisfaction 
 Delayed project delivery  
 Inconsistent customer support  
 Frequent project team changes  
 Slow issue resolution  
Employee Attrition 
 High workload  
 Better opportunities in competing firms  
 Limited career growth  
 Lack of employee engagement  
Observation: High attrition affects project continuity, which further reduces customer 
satisfaction. 
 
Q4. What recommendations would you 
provide to improve operational efficiency and 
profitability? 
Focus Area Recommendation 
Human Resources Improve retention through career development and employee engagement 
Operations Increase resource utilization and strengthen project governance 
Sales Improve lead qualification and reduce sales cycle 
Customer Success Enhance post-project support and collect regular feedback 
Expected Outcome: Lower operating costs, improved customer satisfaction, and higher 
profitability. 
 
Q5. Prepare a strategic roadmap to improve 
EBITDA over the next three years. 
Timeline Key Actions Expected Outcome 
0–6 
Months 
Improve employee retention, strengthen project 
monitoring, enhance customer support 
Reduce attrition and delivery 
delays 
6–18 
Months 
Optimize resource utilization, improve sales 
conversion, standardize project delivery 
Increase operational 
efficiency and customer 
retention 
18–36 
Months 
Expand high-margin consulting services, invest in AI 
and automation, strengthen strategic client 
relationships 
Improve EBITDA margin 
from 11% to 18%

only increasing revenue. Reducing employee attrition, improving project delivery, increasing 
sales effectiveness, and enhancing customer satisfaction will help the company achieve 
sustainable profitability and reach its target EBITDA margin over the next three years.
