title: Digital Patient Experience and Telehealth
question: Analyze the following business challenge: Digital Patient Experience and Telehealth. Outline your structured approach, root cause diagnosis, and recommendations.
solution_approach:
Digital Patient Experience and Telehealth 
Expansion in a Healthcare Network 
Consulting Case Study | Digital Transformation, Healthcare 
Executive Summary (TLDR) 
A regional healthcare network with 18 clinics was struggling with high appointment no-show rates, long 
phone-based scheduling wait times, and underused telehealth capacity built during a prior initiative. A 
digital patient experience transformation redesigned scheduling, communication, and telehealth 
workflows, reducing no-show rates from 22% to 11%, cutting average scheduling call time from 8 
minutes to under 2, and increasing telehealth utilization from 9% to 34% of eligible visits within 12 
months. 
Table of Contents 
● Background 
● Methodology 
● Key Considerations 
● Sample Deliverables 
● Strategic Recommendations 
● Culture and Change Management 
● Technology and Platform Architecture 
● Patient Journey Redesign 
● Regulatory and Privacy Considerations 
● Risk Identification 
● Cost-Benefit Analysis 
● Monitoring and Adoption Metrics 
● Integration with Clinical Systems 
● Return on Investment 
● Establishing a Digital Operating Model 
● Change Management Playbook 
● Additional Considerations 
● Key Findings and FAQs 
1. Background 
A regional healthcare network operating 18 primary and specialty care clinics had invested in telehealth 
capability during a prior initiative, but utilization remained low at just 9% of eligible visits — well below 
the network's own targets and below regional peer benchmarks. Meanwhile, appointment no-show 
rates sat at 22%, driven partly by a phone-only scheduling process with average call wait times of eight 
minutes, which discouraged patients from calling back to reschedule or confirm appointments. 
Clinic staff reported that patients frequently didn't know telehealth was an available option for their 
visit type, and that the scheduling phone line was overwhelmed during peak hours, pushing some 
patients to simply not show up rather than wait on hold. Leadership needed to determine whether 
investment should focus on promoting the existing telehealth capability more heavily, or on a broader 
redesign of the patient scheduling and communication experience that telehealth adoption depended 
on. 
2. Methodology 
A 6-phase digital transformation approach was applied: 
● Phase 1 – Patient Journey Diagnostic: Map the scheduling, reminder, and visit journey to 
identify where patients disengaged or defaulted to no-show. 
● Phase 2 – Telehealth Eligibility Analysis: Determine which visit types were clinically appropriate 
for telehealth and why eligible patients weren't choosing it. 
● Phase 3 – Digital Scheduling Redesign: Build an online scheduling option integrated with clinic 
calendars, reducing dependence on phone-based booking. 
● Phase 4 – Communication Redesign: Implement automated, multi-channel appointment 
reminders and telehealth-option prompts at the point of scheduling. 
● Phase 5 – Phased Clinic Rollout: Pilot the redesigned experience at a subset of clinics before 
network-wide deployment. 
● Phase 6 – Scale & Optimize: Expand to all clinics and continuously refine based on no-show and 
utilization data. 
3. Key Considerations 
● Low telehealth utilization wasn't primarily an awareness problem — it was a default problem: 
patients weren't being offered telehealth as an option at the point of scheduling for eligible visit 
types. 
● No-show rates were closely tied to scheduling friction; patients who couldn't easily reschedule 
when their circumstances changed simply didn't show up rather than navigating a long phone 
wait. 
● Older patient populations required a digital scheduling experience that didn't assume high 
digital literacy, alongside continued phone support rather than a phone-line replacement. 
4. Sample Deliverables 
● Patient journey diagnostic with no-show driver analysis 
● Telehealth eligibility criteria and default-offer framework 
● Online scheduling platform integration plan 
● Automated multi-channel reminder and communication workflow 
● Clinic-level rollout and adoption tracking dashboard 
5. Strategic Recommendations 
The recommended approach centered on three changes: (1) implementing online self-scheduling 
integrated with clinic calendars to reduce dependence on the overwhelmed phone line; (2) defaulting 
eligible visit types to offer telehealth as an explicit choice at the point of scheduling rather than 
requiring patients to ask for it; and (3) replacing single-channel appointment reminders with automated 
text, email, and app notifications including one-tap rescheduling. 
6. Culture and Change Management 
Clinic front-desk staff were concerned that online scheduling would reduce their role and create 
confusion if patients booked inappropriate appointment types. The program addressed this by 
positioning online scheduling as a capacity release valve for phone staff — reducing call volume so staff 
could spend more time on complex scheduling needs and patient support — with clear escalation paths 
built into the online system for ambiguous cases. 
7. Technology and Platform Architecture 
An online scheduling platform was integrated directly with existing clinic calendar systems, allowing 
real-time appointment booking without manual reconciliation by front-desk staff. Automated 
communication workflows were layered on top to handle reminders and telehealth prompts based on 
visit type and patient history. 
8. Patient Journey Redesign 
The scheduling journey was redesigned so that telehealth-eligible visit types presented telehealth as a 
default, equally prominent option alongside in-person scheduling, rather than an obscure alternative 
patients had to specifically request. 
9. Regulatory and Privacy Considerations 
The telehealth and digital scheduling platforms were implemented in full compliance with applicable 
healthcare privacy regulations, with particular attention to secure video-visit infrastructure and patient 
data handling across the newly integrated scheduling and communication systems. 
10. Risk Identification 
Key risks included the possibility of increased no-shows if online scheduling made booking too 
frictionless without adequate reminder follow-up, clinical risk if patients selected telehealth for visit 
types requiring in-person examination, and the risk of alienating less digitally comfortable patients. Each 
was mitigated through automated reminder sequencing, clinically validated eligibility rules, and 
continued phone-support availability. 
11. Cost-Benefit Analysis 
Platform investment was weighed against the value of reduced no-show-related revenue loss, reduced 
phone-staffing pressure, and better utilization of existing telehealth infrastructure that had already been 
paid for but underused. The business case showed payback within the first year primarily through no-
show reduction. 
12. Monitoring and Adoption Metrics 
No-show rate, average scheduling call time, telehealth utilization rate, and online scheduling adoption 
were tracked weekly during the pilot phase, allowing rapid identification of clinics or visit types where 
the redesigned journey wasn't performing as expected. 
13. Integration with Clinical Systems 
The scheduling and communication platforms were integrated with the network's electronic health 
record (EHR) system to ensure visit-type eligibility rules and patient history were reflected accurately in 
real time, avoiding scheduling errors that could create clinical risk. 
14. Return on Investment 
Within 12 months, no-show rates fell from 22% to 11%, average scheduling call time dropped from eight 
minutes to under two, and telehealth utilization rose from 9% to 34% of eligible visits, substantially 
improving both patient access and clinic operational efficiency. 
15. Establishing a Digital Operating Model 
A Patient Digital Experience team was established, combining clinical operations, IT, and patient 
communications representation, to sustain ongoing optimization of scheduling and telehealth adoption 
beyond the initial rollout. 
16. Change Management Playbook 
A playbook was developed for front-desk staff transitioning toward higher-value patient support roles, 
along with a phased clinic rollout sequence and patient communication materials introducing the new 
scheduling and telehealth options. 
17. Additional Considerations 
The platform architecture was designed to support future expansion into chronic condition remote 
monitoring and asynchronous digital visits, building on the scheduling and communication foundation 
established in this phase. 
18. Key Findings and FAQs 
Why was telehealth utilization so low despite prior investment? Because eligible visit types weren't 
defaulting patients toward the telehealth option at the point of scheduling — the capability existed but 
wasn't being actively offered. 
What had the single biggest impact on no-show reduction? Automated, multi-channel reminders with 
one-tap rescheduling, which let patients easily adjust plans instead of simply not showing up. 
How was clinical safety maintained while expanding telehealth defaults? Through clinically validated 
eligibility rules embedded directly into the scheduling system, ensuring only appropriate visit types were 
offered telehealth by default.

solution_approach:
One of America’s leading beverage manufacturers was 
established decades ago when an inspired innovator started 
bottling drinks for thirsty local consumers. The company 
quickly bubbled up into a well-recognized empire known 
for its creative and satisfying refreshment. After years of 
growth, innovation and commitment to quality, the company 
is now worth billions.
During the COVID-19 global pandemic, consumers’ drinking 
increased in volume, beverage preferences shifted, and 
sales skyrocketed for this manufacturer. In 2020, people 
were quarantining and leading more sedentary lives, and 
looking for healthier beverage options — resulting in 
increased sales across the company’s lower-calorie 
beverage offerings. As pandemic restrictions continued 
into 2021, the company’s lower-calorie brands consistently 
saw double-digit growth.
In early 2022, as stores and restaurants reopened, 
consumer preferences shifted again and sales slumped 
industry-wide. The resulting dip in sales for this 
manufacturer suggested they needed to reevaluate their 
supply chain strategy for a post-pandemic world.
The better the question
Can a thirst for efficiencies also 
help satisfy customer demand?
A supply chain transformation cut operational 
costs by centralizing real-time customer data.
1
Client case study
How a flexible supply 
chain raised the bar for 
the beverage industry
“Balancing supply and demand throughout the pandemic 
taught us we needed an agile sales and supply chain strategy 
that could meet rapidly evolving consumer needs, keep pace 
with shifting market demands, and produce higher quantities 
and varieties of products,” said a company operations 
executive. “To stay competitive, we wanted a novel supply 
chain strategy, refurbished IT infrastructure, and additional 
investment and training for our dedicated employees.”
This national beverage manufacturer chose to collaborate 
with an Ernst & Young LLP (EY) team of 
supply chain 
professionals to develop an innovative, data-driven 
supply chain solution that could better accommodate 
future growth, effectively predict the demands of a 
dynamic beverage market, upskill their workforce, and 
meet consumer demands with agile inventory and 
production lines.
The client’s goal: better accommodate 
future growth, predict customer 
demands, and add agility to inventory 
and production lines.
The better the answer
Refreshed technology reduces costs 
and increases efficiencies
Robotic process automation and artificial 
intelligence tune up services at the DMV. 2
With the goal of revolutionizing its supply chain strategy, 
this manufacturer embarked on a nearly 24-month voyage 
with EY teams to identify new efficiencies for each link in 
its supply chain, and developed a solution to better align 
supply with demand for all products across their multiple 
US factories. Together, they would improve IT analytics 
systems to more accurately predict and respond to shifting 
demands for different beverages and more efficiently 
produce the variety of products needed to cater to a 
growing range of consumer preferences, all while investing 
more in their employees.
First, the company’s primary manufacturing site installed 
two new aluminum packaging lines to support increasing 
consumer demand. The EY Run-to-Target (RTT) 
Transformation Accelerator was applied to achieve rapid 
results and encourage sustainable change. RTT helped 
increase production and capacity at this location, which 
became critical when the main bottle line at another factory 
was shut down to install a new pasteurizer. The efficiency 
of the RTT at the primary location allowed the company 
to shift production there, while the other site shut down 
temporarily, thus avoiding a need to outsource production 
to meet customer demand.
The company integrated agility into its processes by 
reducing batch sizes to meet more realistic inventory 
targets. By producing smaller batches and enabling faster 
changeovers, the company could meet shipment and 
customer demands without exceeding inventory allowances. 
Because of this, the company could now effectively manage 
liquid changeovers while addressing long-term supply chain 
needs and avoiding excess inventory.
Leadership at the beverage manufacturer knew that 
upgraded technology and data utilization would only 
achieve lasting success if they were paired with training 
and employee investment. “We drove adoption at all 
levels, starting at the C-suite,” said a company operations 
executive. “We knew if we didn’t have top-level buy-in, 
the program could fizzle. We trained our people on the 
new technologies and processes and aligned teams at 
every level of the operation to company goals.”
The company was able to further empower its employees by 
utilizing the 
EY-P&G Alliance and applying P&G’s Integrated 
Work System (IWS) across their formulating, blending, 
packaging, and warehousing operations. This new operating 
system helped to realign output and inventory management 
and relies on employee engagement to synchronize the 
workforce under one streamlined operating model.
“Our industry used to believe longer runs were more 
efficient and that automation increased productivity, but 
that’s no longer how we stay competitive into 2024,” says 
a company board member. “Our supply chain now uses a 
dynamic production strategy to maximize operational 
efficiency, applies market data to help us stay ahead of 
consumer trends, has an upgraded IT infrastructure to 
provide leadership with more in-depth data reports, and 
relies on our talented employees to help us achieve 
operational excellence.”
Top executives worked alongside the 
manufacturing team to help encourage 
adoption of our new ways of working. 
Even the company’s founder took part 
in hands-on work on the shop floor. 
Company operations executive
“
The supply chain transformation for this beverage 
powerhouse, facilitated in partnership with EY and P&G, 
continues to help the company remain a national industry 
leader. Currently operating as a full-capacity beverage 
manufacturer and distributor across 50 states, the 
company has the flexibility to adapt based on product 
performance and consumer demand.
“We continue to reduce changeover time and increase 
efficiency across our factories — defining new standards 
and improving equipment reliability,” added a company 
operations executive. “And when our new equipment 
reaches optimum volume, it will increase case production 
by more than four times.”
The company’s comprehensive supply chain solution has 
already yielded notable results:
 300+ wholesalers/distributors/retailers effectively 
served thanks to boosted line performance from 
the RTT.
 Millions of cases filled more efficiently on an 
annual basis.
 30% reduction in changeover times across affected 
factories.
 18% increase in bottle and can throughput annually.
 100% workforce engagement using IWS.
 Significant increase in equipment effectiveness.
The better the world works
A more effective operating model keeps 
business flowing
EY consultants and alliances helped align skills and supply 
to meet demand for cost savings and crisp refreshment. 3
This American beverage manufacturer is now operating with 
fewer interruptions, maintaining efficiency across production 
lines, meeting consumer demands with precision, and 
increasing sales cycles. The company maintains that 
increasing operational excellence involves more than just 
improved systems and technology; training and employee 
engagement will remain a central component of their overall 
supply chain solution.
As they embark on the next phase of their transformation, 
the company plans to focus on refining their manufacturing 
strategy further through IWS and new technology such as 
automated storage retrieval systems. Thirsty to push 
boundaries, they are also committed to their long-term 
growth strategy of creating new innovative beverages that 
hopefully will continue exceeding consumer expectations for 
years to come.

supply chain solution that could better accommodate 
future growth, effectively predict the demands of a 
dynamic beverage market, upskill their workforce, and 
meet consumer demands with agile inventory and 
production lines.

with EY teams to identify new efficiencies for each link in 
its supply chain, and developed a solution to better align 
supply with demand for all products across their multiple 
US factories. Together, they would improve IT analytics 
systems to more accurately predict and respond to shifting 
demands for different beverages and more efficiently 
produce the variety of products needed to cater to a 
growing range of consumer preferences, all while investing 
more in their employees.

two new aluminum packaging lines to support increasing 
consumer demand. The EY Run-to-Target (RTT)

increase production and capacity at this location, which

1

09/07/2025, 21:50 Enabling better decision-making and optimizing the military’s workforce | EY - US
https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/government-public-sector/enabling-better-decision-making-and-optimizing-the-military-workforce 1/8
Military bases are much more than barracks. Many of them have the
populations and infrastructures of small cities, with properties
ranging from buildings, fences, water lines, electric lines, parking lots,
sidewalks and fire hydrants to cemeteries and hospitals. One military
command, which manages the installation’s day-to-day operations,
needs to track hundreds of thousands of facilities and nearly $400
billion in assets through its property management systems.
Accurately recording the property is a massive undertaking with vital
importance for military decision-making. Simply keeping track of
thousands of military buildings, facilities and structures alone would
be a difficult task, but the complexity is multiplied by the rigorous
accounting that the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) requires for
each individual asset. The DoD requires commands to report and
manage over 50 data elements for every one of their assets, making
organizations responsible for reporting on millions of data points and
there’s little room for error. With DoD leadership using property
management systems data to create budgets, plan exercises and
assess construction needs, accurate data is crucial to the
management of the military’s real estate.
But these inventories aren’t reliable. Inspections have relied on a
labor-heavy, inconsistent and decentralized process where inspection
information was entered manually into a variety of forms, including
Word documents, paper slips, spreadsheets and handwritten notes,
that would be saved as pdf documents and stored offline with
inconsistent formatting — creating a near-constant risk of user error.
Simple checks showed that the military’s inventory records didn’t
accurately reflect reality. Basic information about a building, including
its physical condition, square footage or the type of structure, could
be incorrect. In one instance, a property listed as a garrison
09/07/2025, 21:50 Enabling better decision-making and optimizing the military’s workforce | EY - US
https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/government-public-sector/enabling-better-decision-making-and-optimizing-the-military-workforce 2/8
headquarters actually was a day care center, while other inspections
showed that buildings listed as active were boarded up and without
running water, or they simply did not exist.
In 2019, EY professionals teamed with a DoD property command to
streamline processes, aiming to reduce the administrative burden on
the workforce and provide military leadership with the accuracy
needed for informed decision-making. EY professionals cleaned up
the organization’s data records and sped up its physical inventory
process, saving over 150,000 workforce hours in the first nine
months of implementation. The recovered workforce time represented
millions of saved taxpayer dollars. By replacing the inconsistent and
time-consuming manual process, EY personnel helped optimize the
military’s workforce and enabled better decision-making among its
leadership.
2
 The better the answer

truth
Through digital tools, the EY team improved
the accuracy, reduced the burden on the
workforces and provided new tools to military
leadership.
09/07/2025, 21:50 Enabling better decision-making and optimizing the military’s workforce | EY - US
https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/government-public-sector/enabling-better-decision-making-and-optimizing-the-military-workforce 3/8
The EY team created consistency in all stages of the inventory
documentation process by using an automated management solution
that was configured by EY technology consultants. Through a
combination of robotic process automation (RPA), optical character
recognition (OCR) technology, Power BI and Pega Business Process
Management (BPM) software, the EY team created an easily
configurable, user-friendly portable solution that delivered a seamless
experience so users could see data, access the application and edit
information, upload photos or scan documentation to asset records
via mobile devices. Through built-in validation, the Pega application
forced standardization into data input and eliminated the risk of
confusion. Users had to complete all required fields before they could
move on. If they tried to enter a four-digit code into a field requiring
five digits, they couldn’t access the next page, making it clear that
they were not adding the required information.
With the property record data collection process cleaned up, RPA
technology and OCR software made it easier for the DoD’s leadership
to put that data into action. Using RPA, a bot took the approved data
from the BPM software to update the property records in an
enterprise resource planning tool — the central storehouse of property
records — enabling an automated process designed to quickly
generate reports that accurately reflect data in the field. When the
DoD’s leadership needed supporting documentation for decision-
making, bots and OCR auto-populated the required government
forms, replacing an error-prone manual process.
09/07/2025, 21:50 Enabling better decision-making and optimizing the military’s workforce | EY - US
https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/government-public-sector/enabling-better-decision-making-and-optimizing-the-military-workforce 4/8
Working with the configurable low-code Pega system, the EY team
used the software in a visionary way and pushed the boundaries of its
capabilities. Initially, the goal wasn’t having it as a complete suite of
solutions ready at the start, but instead to offer a viable product that
could be tested, expanded and improved as needed during a series of
two-week testing and deployment sprints.
The goal was to create a tool any user could pick up and start using
immediately, without great risk of error, e.g., using a simple
screwdriver, not a table saw. To reach the desired ease of use, the tool
was shaped by the experiences of the people using it. The EY team led
the designers through iterative updates in a series of two-week
sprints, drawing on the feedback from users. Pega’s BPM is low code
and designed to be easily configured, allowing developers to quickly
adapt it to client needs without resorting to hours spent writing
complicated code. If users reported that something in the interface
was inconvenient, counterintuitive or buggy, that critique would drive

boundaries

the EY team created a technology solution

accurate.

the team’s focus for the next two-week sprint update. With each
iteration, the tool grew more intuitive.
This story shows how agile thinking and innovations in military tech
can unlock unexpected value. Through simplified inventory recording,
leadership could redirect its workforce from time-consuming low-level
tasks that support the mission’s resources to more valuable, mission-

title: Digital Network Modernization &
question: Analyze the following business challenge: Digital Network Modernization &. Outline your structured approach, root cause diagnosis, and recommendations.
solution_approach:
Digital Network Modernization & 
Customer Experience Overhaul for a 
Telecom Operator 
Consulting Case Study | Telecom Industry 
Reading time: 9 minutes 
Executive Summary (TLDR) 
A national telecom operator was losing postpaid subscribers to a smaller, digitally native competitor 
despite having superior network coverage. Legacy OSS/BSS systems, slow provisioning times, and a 
fragmented customer experience across app, call center, and retail were driving churn. A structured 
network-and-CX transformation program cut new-service provisioning time from 5 days to 4 hours, 
reduced churn by 1.8 percentage points, and lifted digital self-service adoption from 31% to 58% within 
15 months. 
Table of Contents 
● Background 
● Methodology 
● Key Considerations 
● Sample Deliverables 
● Strategic Recommendations 
● Culture and Change Management 
● Technology and OSS/BSS Modernization 
● Operational Efficiency 
● Regulatory Considerations 
● Risk Identification 
● Cost-Benefit Analysis 
● Monitoring and KPIs 
● Integration Roadmap 
● Return on Investment 
● Establishing Governance 
● Implementation Playbook 
● Additional Considerations 
● Key Findings and FAQs 
1. Background 
A national telecom operator with strong network coverage and brand recognition began losing postpaid 
subscribers at an accelerating rate — down 1.8 points in market share over six quarters — despite 
consistently outperforming competitors in network quality surveys. Customer research revealed the 
issue wasn't the network; it was everything around it. Activating a new line took up to five business days 
due to manual provisioning steps across disconnected legacy OSS (Operations Support Systems) and BSS 
(Business Support Systems). Customers switching plans often experienced billing errors for one to two 
cycles. The mobile app covered only basic functions, pushing most service requests to call centers with 
average wait times exceeding 12 minutes. 
A smaller, digitally native competitor with weaker network coverage was winning switchers specifically 
because activation, plan changes, and support were instant and self-service. Leadership needed to 
determine whether to prioritize a full OSS/BSS replacement — expensive and high-risk — or a more 
targeted modernization of the systems and journeys causing the most customer pain. 
2. Methodology 
A 6-phase approach combining operational and digital transformation methodology was applied: 
● Phase 1 – Diagnostic & Journey Mapping: Quantify friction points across activation, plan 
changes, billing, and support using both system data and customer interviews. 
● Phase 2 – Prioritization: Rank pain points by combined customer impact and technical 
feasibility, rather than pursuing a full system replacement. 
● Phase 3 – Target Architecture Design: Design a modernized provisioning layer that could sit 
atop legacy OSS/BSS via APIs, avoiding a full "rip and replace." 
● Phase 4 – Journey Redesign: Rebuild the top five customer journeys (activation, plan change, 
billing dispute, device upgrade, outage reporting) for digital-first resolution. 
● Phase 5 – Phased Rollout: Deploy market-by-market to manage risk and capture learnings 
before national rollout. 
● Phase 6 – Scale & Optimize: Expand successful patterns nationally and retire redundant manual 
processes. 
3. Key Considerations 
● A full legacy system replacement was rejected as too risky and slow given competitive pressure; 
an API-layer approach delivered most of the customer-facing benefit at a fraction of the cost 
and time. 
● Provisioning delays were traced to seven manual handoff points between systems that had 
accumulated over a decade of incremental patches — the fix required both technology and 
process redesign. 
● Call-center staff needed a clear transition plan, since reduced call volume from improved self-
service directly affected their role. 
4. Sample Deliverables 
● Customer journey friction diagnostic and prioritization matrix 
● API-layer target architecture blueprint (legacy-compatible) 
● Redesigned digital journeys for activation, plan change, billing, and support 
● Phased market rollout plan with success criteria per wave 
● Call-center transition and reskilling plan 
5. Strategic Recommendations 
The recommended path avoided a full OSS/BSS replacement in favor of an API orchestration layer that 
automated the manual handoffs causing provisioning delays, paired with a redesigned mobile app 
covering the top customer journeys end-to-end. This combination addressed 80% of customer pain 
points within a fraction of the time and cost of full system replacement, while preserving the option for 
deeper modernization later. 
6. Culture and Change Management 
Call-center leadership initially resisted the shift toward self-service, viewing reduced call volume as a 
threat to their teams. The program reframed the transition around redeploying staff toward complex, 
high-value support cases — the ones self-service couldn't resolve — with a structured reskilling plan 
rather than headcount reduction, which secured buy-in from frontline leadership. 
7. Technology and OSS/BSS Modernization 
Rather than replacing legacy OSS/BSS systems outright, an orchestration layer was built to automate the 
seven manual handoff points in the provisioning process, cutting activation time from five days to under 
four hours while legacy systems remained the system of record underneath. 
8. Operational Efficiency 
Automating manual provisioning steps eliminated a significant volume of internal rework caused by 
human error in the handoff process, which had previously been a major driver of billing disputes in the 
first two cycles after any account change. 
9. Regulatory Considerations 
Billing accuracy improvements were tracked against regulatory requirements for consumer billing 
transparency, with the redesigned billing dispute journey built to meet documented resolution-timeline 
requirements consistently, which had previously been missed during peak volume periods. 
10. Risk Identification 
Key risks included the possibility of new customer-facing bugs during phased rollout, the risk of over-
automating and removing necessary human judgment in edge cases, and the risk of call-center attrition 
if the transition plan wasn't communicated clearly. Each was mitigated through phased deployment, 
defined escalation paths, and early, transparent staff communication. 
11. Cost-Benefit Analysis 
The API orchestration approach cost roughly a third of a full OSS/BSS replacement while delivering the 
majority of customer-facing improvement. The business case showed payback within 18 months driven 
by reduced churn and lower call-center cost-to-serve. 
12. Monitoring and KPIs 
Core KPIs tracked weekly included activation time, digital self-service adoption rate, first-cycle billing 
accuracy, call-center volume, and churn rate — allowing the team to validate impact market by market 
before national rollout. 
13. Integration Roadmap 
Rollout proceeded in three waves — two pilot markets, a mid-size regional expansion, and finally 
national deployment — with each wave's KPIs reviewed before proceeding, allowing course correction 
on journey design based on real usage data. 
14. Return on Investment 
Within 15 months, provisioning time dropped from five days to four hours, churn improved by 1.8 
percentage points, and digital self-service adoption rose from 31% to 58%, with call-center cost-to-serve 
down significantly as a result. 
15. Establishing Governance 
A joint IT-Operations-Customer Experience steering committee was established to own the 
transformation, ensuring technology, process, and frontline considerations were represented in every 
major rollout decision. 
16. Implementation Playbook 
A standardized market-rollout playbook was created covering technical deployment checklists, staff 
training sequencing, and customer communication timing, reducing variability in how each new market 
wave was executed. 
17. Additional Considerations 
The orchestration-layer approach was explicitly designed to be a stepping stone — architected so that a 
future full OSS/BSS modernization, if pursued, could build on the same API layer rather than requiring 
another disruptive redesign. 
18. Key Findings and FAQs 
Why not replace the legacy systems outright? The risk, cost, and timeline of a full replacement didn't 
match the urgency of the competitive threat; the orchestration-layer approach delivered comparable 
customer impact far faster. 
What was the single biggest driver of churn reduction? Faster activation and plan-change times, which 
directly addressed the primary reason customers cited for switching to the digital-native competitor. 
Is this approach reusable for other operators with legacy systems? Yes — the API orchestration pattern 
is broadly applicable wherever legacy system replacement is too risky to attempt in the required 
timeframe.

title: Cybersecurity Transformation
question:
What are the most 
significant operational and cyber risks facing the org anization? How effectively are these risks currently 
managed, and where does ownership sit today? 
Phase 2 — Target Operating Model Design 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
4 
Define the future -state cybersecurity operating model, including organizational structure, reporting lines, 
decision rights, and the interface between corporate security, IT, and business units. 
Phase 3 — Strategy and Roadmap Development 
Translate the assessment into a prioritized, sequenced roadmap of initiatives across a 12 -month horizon, 
aligned to risk severity, regulatory exposure, and resource availability. 
Phase 4 — Control Design and Playbook Development 
Build the control frameworks, incident response playbooks, and technical standards required to close 
identified gaps, including identity and access management, vendor risk, and detection and response 
capability. 
Phase 5 — Pilot and Phased Rollout 
Implement priority initiatives in a controlled sequence, beginning with the highest -severity gaps and the 
business units most exposed to regulatory or reputational risk. 
Phase 6 — Embed, Monitor, and Mature 
Institutionalize governance forums, metrics, and continuous monitoring so risk management becomes a 
standing operational discipline rather than a one-time project. 
3. Key Considerations 
Several considerations shaped how the engagement was scoped and sequenced: 
• Speed versus rigor: the business was under pressure to keep expanding, so the roadmap had to 
demonstrate quick wins within 90 days without appearing to slow growth. 
• M&A integration debt: each acquired entity brought its own systems, vendors, and risk posture, 
requiring a standardized due-diligence and integration checklist for future deals. 
• Customer trust and brand exposure: a retailer's cybersecurity posture is closely tied to customer-facing 
trust; incidents involving payment data or personal information carry outsized reputational risk relative 
to their technical severity. 
• Resource constraints: the existing security team of six was sized for the pre -expansion business and 
lacked specialized skills in cloud security, e-commerce fraud, and third-party risk management. 
• Board and regulatory visibility: the attorney general inquiry meant several workstreams had to produce 
evidence of remediation on a defined timeline, not just directional progress. 
4. Sample Deliverables 
The engagement produced a structured set of deliverables designed to be both immediately actionable and 
durable beyond the consulting engagement: 
• Cybersecurity Operating Model (target-state org design, RACI, and governance charter) 
• Enterprise Risk Register with likelihood/impact scoring across 40+ identified risks 
• 12-Month Cybersecurity Strategy and Roadmap with 18 prioritized initiatives 
• Incident Response Playbooks (payment data compromise, ransomware, third-party data exposure) 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
5 
• Third-Party and Vendor Risk Management Framework and onboarding questionnaire 
• PCI-DSS Scoping and Remediation Plan for the mobile app payment flow 
• Executive and Board Reporting Dashboard (KPI/KRI pack) 
• M&A Cybersecurity Due Diligence Checklist for future acquisitions 
 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
6 
5. Strategic Alignment and Executive Sponsorship 
A recurring pattern in fast -growing retailers is that cybersecurity investment lags revenue growth until a 
visible incident forces the issue onto the board agenda. At Meridian, the CFO and Chief Digital Officer had 
been the primary sponsors of expansion; security had no seat at that table. 
The engagement's first strategic move was establishing a Cybersecurity Steering Committee chaired by the 
COO, with standing representation from Finance, Digital, Merchandising, and Legal. This gave security a 
forum to weigh in on expansion decisions — new marketplace launches, vendor selection, and acquisition 
targets — before they were finalized rather than after an incident. 
A one-page “cyber risk appetite statement” was drafted and approved by the board, defining acceptable risk 
thresholds for categories such as payment data handling, third -party access, and downtime tolerance for 
fulfillment systems. This gave business teams  a clear, pre -agreed boundary to plan within, rather than 
requiring case-by-case security sign-off that was often perceived as a bottleneck. 
Executive Alignment Outcomes 
• Security became a standing agenda item at monthly executive reviews, not just quarterly board 
meetings.

TECHNOLOGY CONSULTING CASE STUDY  
Cybersecurity Transformation 
in Omnichannel Retail 
Building Enterprise-Grade Security Into a Rapidly Scaling E-Commerce Platform 
CLIENT 
Meridian Retail Group — mid-market omnichannel apparel & home goods retailer 
ENGAGEMENT FOCUS 
Cybersecurity operating model, risk assessment, and 12-month security roadmap following rapid digital 
and geographic expansion 
READING TIME 
12 minutes 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
2 
Table of Contents 
1. Background 
2. Methodology 
3. Key Considerations 
4. Sample Deliverables 
5. Strategic Alignment and Executive Sponsorship 
6. Culture and Change Management 
7. Technology Architecture and Tool Selection 
8. Operational Resilience and Incident Response 
9. Regulatory and Compliance Considerations 
10. Risk Identification and Prioritization 
11. Cost-Benefit Analysis 
12. Monitoring and Continuous Improvement 
13. Integration with Business Strategy 
14. Return on Investment 
15. Establishing Metrics and KPIs 
16. Governance Structure and Operating Model 
17. Additional Considerations 
18. Key Findings and Results 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
3 
1. Background 
Consider this scenario: a mid-market omnichannel retailer is grappling with escalating cybersecurity risk 
following an 18-month period of rapid expansion that has not been matched by its security capabilities. 
Meridian Retail Group is a mid-market apparel and home goods retailer generating roughly $1.4B in annual 
revenue across brick -and-mortar stores, a direct -to-consumer e-commerce site, a mobile app, and third -
party marketplace storefronts. Over the prior 18 months, the company acquired two smaller regional 
retailers, launched storefronts on two major marketplaces, expanded into the UK and EU, and rolled out a 
new mobile app with integrated digital wallet and buy-now-pay-later functionality. 
This growth was not accompanied by a corresponding investment in security architecture, governance, or 
staffing. The result was a fragmented technology environment: newly acquired subsidiaries retained legacy 
point-of-sale systems, marketplace integrations  were built quickly by third -party developers with limited 
security review, and the mobile app's payment flow was launched ahead of a completed PCI-DSS assessment. 
Within a six-month window, the company experienced three material incidents: a credential-stuffing attack 
against customer accounts during a holiday promotional period, a ransomware attempt against a distribution 
center that was contained but caused a two -day fulfillment slowdown, and a vendor -side data exposure 
involving a third -party marketing platform holding customer email and purchase history. None of these 
individually caused catastrophic damage, but together they drew board-level attention and a formal inquiry 
from a state attorney general's office. 
Working Hypotheses 
The organization's expansion outpaced its risk management processes, suggesting the underlying issues 
could be inadequate risk identification and outdated control mechanisms inherited through acquisition. 
Three hypotheses were tested during the initial assessment: 
• Fragmented governance: security decisions were being made independently by business unit and IT 
teams with no unified operating model or risk ownership at the executive level. 
• Inherited technical debt: acquired subsidiaries and rapidly built integrations carried outdated controls, 
unpatched systems, and inconsistent identity and access management. 
• Insufficient integration into strategy: cybersecurity was treated as a compliance checkbox rather than 
a factor in expansion, vendor selection, and product launch decisions. 
2. Methodology 
A 6-phase approach to cybersecurity transformation was proposed for the organization, structured to move 
from diagnosis to embedded, sustainable operating practice. 
Phase 1 — Comprehensive Risk Assessment 
Identify and evaluate risk across people, process, and technology domains spanning corporate IT, store 
systems, e -commerce infrastructure, and third -party integrations. Key questions: What are the most 
significant operational and cyber risks facing the org anization? How effectively are these risks currently 
managed, and where does ownership sit today? 
Phase 2 — Target Operating Model Design 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
4 
Define the future -state cybersecurity operating model, including organizational structure, reporting lines, 
decision rights, and the interface between corporate security, IT, and business units. 
Phase 3 — Strategy and Roadmap Development 
Translate the assessment into a prioritized, sequenced roadmap of initiatives across a 12 -month horizon, 
aligned to risk severity, regulatory exposure, and resource availability. 
Phase 4 — Control Design and Playbook Development 
Build the control frameworks, incident response playbooks, and technical standards required to close 
identified gaps, including identity and access management, vendor risk, and detection and response 
capability. 
Phase 5 — Pilot and Phased Rollout 
Implement priority initiatives in a controlled sequence, beginning with the highest -severity gaps and the 
business units most exposed to regulatory or reputational risk. 
Phase 6 — Embed, Monitor, and Mature 
Institutionalize governance forums, metrics, and continuous monitoring so risk management becomes a 
standing operational discipline rather than a one-time project. 
3. Key Considerations 
Several considerations shaped how the engagement was scoped and sequenced: 
• Speed versus rigor: the business was under pressure to keep expanding, so the roadmap had to 
demonstrate quick wins within 90 days without appearing to slow growth. 
• M&A integration debt: each acquired entity brought its own systems, vendors, and risk posture, 
requiring a standardized due-diligence and integration checklist for future deals. 
• Customer trust and brand exposure: a retailer's cybersecurity posture is closely tied to customer-facing 
trust; incidents involving payment data or personal information carry outsized reputational risk relative 
to their technical severity. 
• Resource constraints: the existing security team of six was sized for the pre -expansion business and 
lacked specialized skills in cloud security, e-commerce fraud, and third-party risk management. 
• Board and regulatory visibility: the attorney general inquiry meant several workstreams had to produce 
evidence of remediation on a defined timeline, not just directional progress. 
4. Sample Deliverables 
The engagement produced a structured set of deliverables designed to be both immediately actionable and 
durable beyond the consulting engagement: 
• Cybersecurity Operating Model (target-state org design, RACI, and governance charter) 
• Enterprise Risk Register with likelihood/impact scoring across 40+ identified risks 
• 12-Month Cybersecurity Strategy and Roadmap with 18 prioritized initiatives 
• Incident Response Playbooks (payment data compromise, ransomware, third-party data exposure) 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
5 
• Third-Party and Vendor Risk Management Framework and onboarding questionnaire 
• PCI-DSS Scoping and Remediation Plan for the mobile app payment flow 
• Executive and Board Reporting Dashboard (KPI/KRI pack) 
• M&A Cybersecurity Due Diligence Checklist for future acquisitions 
 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
6 
5. Strategic Alignment and Executive Sponsorship 
A recurring pattern in fast -growing retailers is that cybersecurity investment lags revenue growth until a 
visible incident forces the issue onto the board agenda. At Meridian, the CFO and Chief Digital Officer had 
been the primary sponsors of expansion; security had no seat at that table. 
The engagement's first strategic move was establishing a Cybersecurity Steering Committee chaired by the 
COO, with standing representation from Finance, Digital, Merchandising, and Legal. This gave security a 
forum to weigh in on expansion decisions — new marketplace launches, vendor selection, and acquisition 
targets — before they were finalized rather than after an incident. 
A one-page “cyber risk appetite statement” was drafted and approved by the board, defining acceptable risk 
thresholds for categories such as payment data handling, third -party access, and downtime tolerance for 
fulfillment systems. This gave business teams  a clear, pre -agreed boundary to plan within, rather than 
requiring case-by-case security sign-off that was often perceived as a bottleneck. 
Executive Alignment Outcomes 
• Security became a standing agenda item at monthly executive reviews, not just quarterly board 
meetings. 
• New vendor and marketplace launches required a documented security review before go-live, reducing 
the recurrence of the type of gap that caused the mobile app payment flow issue. 
• The CISO role was elevated to report directly to the COO rather than to the VP of IT Infrastructure, 
removing a layer that had previously diluted risk visibility. 
6. Culture and Change Management 
Technical controls alone would not have addressed the underlying pattern of security being treated as an 
afterthought. The team ran a culture and awareness workstream in parallel with the technical remediation. 
Store and distribution center employees received targeted training on POS security and physical access 
controls, since the ransomware attempt had entered through a distribution center  vendor laptop with 
excessive network access. Corporate and engineering teams received role -specific training: developers on 
secure coding and API security given the marketplace integration risk, and marketing and CRM teams on 
data handling given the third-party vendor exposure. 
A “security champions” network was established, with one nominated representative in each major product 
and engineering team responsible for surfacing risk earlier in the development lifecycle and acting as a liaison 
to the central security team, which remained understaffed relative to the scale of the technology estate. 
Change Management Risks Identified 
• Initial resistance from engineering teams who viewed new security review gates as a threat to release 
velocity, addressed by setting service -level targets for review turnaround (48 hours for standard 
changes). 
• Store operations staff turnover meant training could not be a one -time event; a recurring onboarding 
module was built into new-hire orientation. 
• Incentive misalignment: business unit bonuses were tied to launch speed with no corresponding metric 
for security review completion, which the steering committee flagged for revision in the following fiscal 
year. 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
7 
7. Technology Architecture and Tool Selection 
The technical environment reflected the company's growth-by-acquisition history: three different point-of-
sale platforms, two identity providers, and a patchwork of marketplace integrations built by different 
external development shops with no shared security standard. 
Rather than a wholesale replatforming, the roadmap prioritized consolidation and control layering over rip-
and-replace, given budget and timeline constraints: 
• Consolidated identity and access management onto a single provider with single sign-on and mandatory 
multi-factor authentication for all corporate and privileged accounts. 
• Deployed a web application firewall and bot-mitigation layer in front of the e-commerce site and mobile 
app APIs to address the credential-stuffing pattern seen during the holiday incident. 
• Implemented endpoint detection and response across corporate and distribution center endpoints, 
replacing legacy antivirus-only coverage. 
• Established a cloud security posture management tool for the AWS environment supporting the e -
commerce platform, which had grown without centralized configuration governance. 
• Standardized a secrets management solution to remove hardcoded API keys found in two of the 
marketplace integrations during the assessment. 
Tool selection favored platforms that integrated with the company's existing SIEM rather than introducing 
additional standalone consoles, given the security team's limited headcount to monitor multiple 
disconnected dashboards. 
8. Operational Resilience and Incident Response 
The distribution center ransomware attempt exposed the absence of a tested incident response process; the 
response that did occur was improvised, and it took nearly 30 hours to determine the scope of affected 
systems. 
Three incident response playbooks were developed, each with defined roles, communication trees, and 
decision checkpoints: unauthorized access to customer accounts, ransomware and business disruption at 
fulfillment sites, and third-party or vendor-side data exposure. Each playbook was tested through a tabletop 
exercise with executive participation, which surfaced gaps in cyber insurance notification timelines and legal 
counsel engagement that had not previously been documented. 
Incident Response Metrics Before and After 
Metric Before Engagement After 12 Months 
Mean time to detect (MTTD) ~48 hours 6.5 hours 
Mean time to contain (MTTR) ~30 hours 4 hours 
Playbooks tested via tabletop exercise 0 3 
Systems with defined incident owner 35% 92% 
9. Regulatory and Compliance Considerations 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
8 
Meridian's expansion into new geographies and payment methods created a compliance footprint the 
organization had not fully mapped: PCI -DSS for card payment handling, GDPR for the UK and EU customer 
base, CCPA/CPRA for California customers, and state breac h-notification statutes across the US markets 
where the acquired subsidiaries operated. 
The attorney general inquiry, triggered by the vendor data exposure incident, required Meridian to 
demonstrate a documented data inventory, a defined incident notification process, and evidence of 
reasonable security measures for personal information — none of which existed in a consolidated form prior 
to the engagement. 
• A data mapping exercise identified seven categories of personal data flowing to seventeen third-party 
vendors, several of which had no data processing agreement in place. 
• The mobile app payment flow was brought into PCI -DSS scope with a remediation plan addressing 
tokenization, network segmentation, and quarterly vulnerability scanning. 
• A breach notification playbook was aligned to the strictest applicable jurisdictional timeline (72 hours 
under GDPR) to avoid maintaining separate response clocks per region. 
10. Risk Identification and Prioritization 
The risk assessment identified 43 distinct risks across the technology estate, scored on likelihood and 
business impact and mapped to the business units and systems affected. A subset of the highest -priority 
risks is illustrated below. 
Risk Likelihood Impact Priority 
Credential stuffing against customer accounts High High Critical 
Unpatched POS systems at acquired subsidiaries High High Critical 
Third-party vendor access without data agreements Medium High High 
Hardcoded API credentials in marketplace 
integrations Medium High High 
Lack of network segmentation at distribution centers Medium High High 
Inconsistent MFA enforcement for privileged 
accounts High Medium High 
Shadow IT tools adopted during rapid expansion Medium Medium Medium 
Prioritization weighted regulatory exposure and customer -facing impact more heavily than pure technical 
severity, reflecting the board's concern with reputational and legal consequences following the attorney 
general inquiry. 
11. Cost-Benefit Analysis 
The 12-month roadmap represented an investment of approximately $3.2M, spanning technology licensing, 
third-party assessment costs, and four incremental security hires. This was evaluated against the estimated 
cost of continued exposure. 
Category Estimated Annual Cost / Exposure 
Roadmap investment (technology, staffing, advisory) $3.2M 
Estimated cost of a single major payment-data breach (industry benchmark) $4.5M – $6.0M 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
9 
Category Estimated Annual Cost / Exposure 
Estimated regulatory fine exposure (GDPR/CCPA, illustrative) $1.0M – $2.5M 
Estimated fulfillment revenue loss per day of distribution center downtime $0.9M 
Cyber insurance premium reduction achieved post-remediation 12% year-over-year 
The steering committee framed the investment less as a cost center and more as insurance against a single 
incident of the scale already experienced twice in the prior six months, which made the business case 
straightforward to approve at the board level. 
 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
10 
12. Monitoring and Continuous Improvement 
A monthly Cybersecurity Risk Review was established, chaired by the CISO and attended by the steering 
committee, tracking the risk register, open remediation items, and key risk indicators. Rather than treating 
the roadmap as a fixed project plan, the revi ew process built in quarterly reprioritization based on new 
threats, new vendor relationships, and any newly acquired business. 
A lightweight internal audit function was introduced to independently validate that controls marked 
“complete” in the tracking system were operating as designed, following an early instance where a control 
was marked closed but had not actually been deployed to one of the acquired subsidiary environments. 
• Quarterly penetration testing was instituted for internet -facing e -commerce and mobile app 
infrastructure, replacing an ad hoc annual test. 
• A vulnerability management SLA was set: critical vulnerabilities remediated within 15 days, high within 
30 days, tracked and reported monthly. 
• Vendor risk reassessment was tied to contract renewal dates rather than a fixed annual cycle, ensuring 
newly onboarded vendors were not left unreviewed for up to a year. 
13. Integration with Business Strategy 
The most durable change from the engagement was procedural rather than technical: cybersecurity review 
was embedded as a formal gate in the company's existing stage -gate process for new initiatives, including 
marketplace launches, geographic expansion, and M&A due diligence. 
For M&A specifically, a Cybersecurity Due Diligence Checklist was built so that any future acquisition target 
would be assessed for security posture, outstanding vulnerabilities, and data handling practices before deal 
close, rather than discovering issues — as had happened with both prior acquisitions — only after integration 
was underway. 
This integration meant that as Meridian continued to plan further international expansion, security 
requirements and estimated remediation costs were now a standard line item in the business case for each 
new market or channel, rather than a downstream retrofit. 
14. Return on Investment 
Return on the cybersecurity investment was measured across three dimensions: risk reduction, operational 
efficiency, and avoided cost. 
Outcome Area Result 
Reduction in operational disruptions linked to security incidents 20% reduction year-over-year 
Overall compliance rate across PCI-DSS, GDPR, and CCPA controls 95% 
Reduction in mean time to detect security incidents ~86% improvement 
Cyber insurance premium 12% reduction 
Critical and high vulnerabilities remediated within SLA 89%, up from an untracked baseline 
While a single avoided breach would have justified the investment on its own, the board placed equal weight 
on the qualitative shift: security had moved from a reactive, incident-driven function to a standing input into 
strategic decision-making. 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
11 
15. Establishing Metrics and KPIs 
A concise set of KPIs and key risk indicators was defined for ongoing board and executive reporting, chosen 
to be understandable to non-technical stakeholders while still meaningful to the security team: 
• Percentage of critical/high vulnerabilities remediated within SLA 
• Mean time to detect and mean time to contain, tracked monthly 
• Percentage of third-party vendors with a current risk assessment on file 
• Number of privileged accounts without MFA enforced 
• Security review completion rate for new product and vendor launches prior to go-live 
• Employee phishing simulation click-through rate, tracked quarterly 
Each metric was assigned an owner and a target threshold, and the full set was consolidated into a single -
page dashboard reviewed monthly by the steering committee, replacing the prior practice of ad hoc, 
incident-triggered reporting to the board. 
16. Governance Structure and Operating Model 
The target -state operating model clarified decision rights that had previously been ambiguous across 
corporate IT, the digital/e-commerce team, and the individual business units inherited through acquisition. 
• Cybersecurity Steering Committee: COO (chair), CISO, CFO, Chief Digital Officer, General Counsel — 
meets monthly, owns risk appetite and cross-functional prioritization. 
• CISO Office: owns the risk register, incident response, vendor risk program, and reports directly to the 
COO. 
• Security Champions Network: one representative per product/engineering team, reporting dotted-line 
to the CISO Office for early risk surfacing. 
• Internal Audit: independently validates control closure and reports findings directly to the Audit 
Committee of the board, separate from the CISO's own reporting line. 
This structure was deliberately designed so that no single function could mark its own homework: the CISO 
Office implemented and tracked controls, while Internal Audit independently verified them — directly 
addressing the earlier instance of a control being marked complete without actually being deployed. 
17. Additional Considerations 
A few additional factors influenced the engagement's design and are worth noting for similar 
transformations in retail and other consumer-facing industries: 
• Seasonality: retail's concentration of revenue and traffic around major shopping events (e.g., Black 
Friday) meant that any control rollout affecting the checkout flow had to be scheduled and tested well 
outside peak season. 
• Franchise and marketplace complexity: security requirements had to be adapted for environments 
Meridian did not fully control, such as marketplace storefronts governed by a third party's platform 
rules.

• Talent market constraints: specialized skills in cloud security and e -commerce fraud were difficult to 
hire directly, leading to a blended model of core in-house staff supplemented by a managed detection 
and response provider.

• How would you structure a market entry strategy for this client?
• What analysis would you prioritize, and why?
• What would your go-to-market plan look like across the three markets?
• How should the company sequence its entry into Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines?
solution_approach:
Case Study on Market Entry 
Strategy
1. Market Entry Strategy – Consumer Goods (FMCG): How an Indian FMCG major can 
structure its expansion into Southeast Asia.
Introduction
An Indian FMCG major with a strong domestic presence is looking to expand into Southeast Asian markets, 
specifically Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Despite its scale and brand strength in India, the company has 
no prior international operating experience. This case study explores how such a company should structure a market 
entry strategy, including the analysis to prioritize and the go-to-market plan to follow.
Background
The Indian FMCG major has built its business on deep distribution networks, strong brand recall, and cost-efficient 
manufacturing within India. With domestic growth beginning to plateau in certain categories, the company's 
leadership has identified Southeast Asia as a natural next step, given the region's growing middle class, rising 
disposable incomes, and cultural and consumption similarities to India.
However, the company faces a limited understanding of local consumer behavior, differing regulatory regimes 
across Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines, and a competitive landscape already dominated by established local 
players and global FMCG giants. Without a structured entry strategy, the company risks costly missteps and slow 
market traction.
Structuring the Market Entry Strategy
• Market Attractiveness Screening- Rank Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines on market size, category 
growth rates, income distribution, and ease of doing business, to decide sequencing rather than entering all 
three simultaneously.
• Consumer Behavior Research- Conduct in-market research on purchasing habits, price sensitivity, preferred 
pack sizes, and channel preferences (general trade versus modern trade versus e-commerce) in each target 
country.
• Regulatory and Compliance Mapping- Assess import duties, local manufacturing incentives, labelling and 
product-registration requirements, and foreign ownership restrictions to determine the most viable legal 
structure.
• Competitive Landscape Assessment- Map incumbent local players and global competitors by category, 
pricing tier, and distribution reach to identify white spaces the company can credibly target.
• Entry Mode Evaluation- Weigh options such as export-led entry, joint ventures with local distributors, 
licensing, or greenfield investment, based on speed to market, capital intensity, and risk appetite.
• Phased Go-to-Market Plan- Start with a focused portfolio of two to three hero products in one lead market, 
build distribution and brand trust, then scale category breadth and geographic footprint in subsequent phases.
Impact
• Reduced Entry Risk- A phased, research-backed approach limits capital exposure while the company builds 
on-ground understanding before scaling.
• Faster Localization- Early investment in consumer and regulatory research helps the company adapt 
packaging, pricing, and messaging to local preferences more quickly than competitors entering blind.
• Sustainable Revenue Growth- A disciplined market and channel prioritization approach improves the odds 
of profitable, repeatable growth rather than one-off wins.
• Reusable Expansion Playbook- The frameworks and learnings from this first expansion create a template the 
company can reapply to future international markets.
Final Note
Successful market entry into Southeast Asia will depend on the company's ability to combine its domestic strengths 
in distribution and brand-building with rigorous, market-specific research. A staged approach that prioritizes 
learning before scale gives the company the best chance of establishing a durable presence in a competitive and 
unfamiliar landscape.
Questions for Discussion
• How would you structure a market entry strategy for this client?
• What analysis would you prioritize, and why?
• What would your go-to-market plan look like across the three markets?
• How should the company sequence its entry into Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines?

question:
• How would you identify and prioritize cost-reduction opportunities across this business?
• Walk through your approach step by step.
• How would you ensure cost cuts do not compromise service quality?
• Which cost levers would you expect to deliver the fastest impact, and which would take longer?
solution_approach:
Case Study on Cost Optimization
2. Cost Optimization – Telecom: How a telecom operator can address margin pressure from 
declining ARPU and rising network costs.
Introduction
A telecom operator is facing significant margin pressure driven by declining average revenue per user (ARPU) and 
rising network operating expenses. This case study explores how the operator can identify and prioritize cost-
reduction opportunities across the business without compromising service quality.
Background
The operator's revenue per user has been steadily declining amid intense price competition and market saturation, 
while network operating expenses continue to climb due to rising data consumption, tower and energy costs, and 
expanding infrastructure requirements. Vendor contracts for network equipment, maintenance, and managed 
services were negotiated several years ago and have not been revisited.
There is currently no structured framework within the organization to systematically identify, evaluate, and 
prioritize cost-saving opportunities, and any past cost-cutting efforts have been ad hoc, raising concern that further 
cuts could degrade network quality and accelerate customer churn.
Approach to Identifying Cost-Reduction Opportunities
• Cost Baseline and Benchmarking- Build a detailed breakdown of network opex (energy, tower leases, 
maintenance, backhaul, managed services) and benchmark each line item against industry peers to size the 
opportunity.
• Vendor Contract Review- Audit existing vendor and managed-services contracts for outdated pricing, 
renegotiate volume-based discounts, and consider multi-vendor bidding to restore competitive tension.
• Network Infrastructure Optimization- Evaluate opportunities such as tower and site sharing with other 
operators, energy-efficient equipment upgrades, and decommissioning of redundant or underutilized sites.
• Zero-Based Cost Framework- Apply a zero-based budgeting lens to non-network costs (customer service, 
back-office, real estate) to challenge legacy spend rather than trimming incrementally.
• Impact vs. Effort Prioritization- Plot identified initiatives on an impact-versus-effort matrix, sequencing 
quick wins (vendor renegotiation) ahead of longer-term structural changes (infrastructure sharing).
• Quality Safeguards- Define minimum service-quality thresholds (network uptime, call drop rates, data 
speeds) that must be protected throughout implementation, with monitoring built into each initiative.
Impact
• Improved Margins- Renegotiated vendor contracts and infrastructure efficiencies directly reduce the cost 
base and help offset ARPU decline.
• Structured Decision-Making- A repeatable cost framework replaces ad hoc cuts, giving leadership a 
consistent way to evaluate future cost initiatives.
• Protected Service Quality- Built-in quality safeguards ensure cost reduction does not come at the expense of

2. Cost Optimization – Telecom: How a telecom operator can address margin pressure from 
declining ARPU and rising network costs.
Introduction
A telecom operator is facing significant margin pressure driven by declining average revenue per user (ARPU) and 
rising network operating expenses. This case study explores how the operator can identify and prioritize cost-
reduction opportunities across the business without compromising service quality.
Background
The operator's revenue per user has been steadily declining amid intense price competition and market saturation, 
while network operating expenses continue to climb due to rising data consumption, tower and energy costs, and 
expanding infrastructure requirements. Vendor contracts for network equipment, maintenance, and managed 
services were negotiated several years ago and have not been revisited.
There is currently no structured framework within the organization to systematically identify, evaluate, and 
prioritize cost-saving opportunities, and any past cost-cutting efforts have been ad hoc, raising concern that further 
cuts could degrade network quality and accelerate customer churn.
Approach to Identifying Cost-Reduction Opportunities
• Cost Baseline and Benchmarking- Build a detailed breakdown of network opex (energy, tower leases, 
maintenance, backhaul, managed services) and benchmark each line item against industry peers to size the 
opportunity.
• Vendor Contract Review- Audit existing vendor and managed-services contracts for outdated pricing, 
renegotiate volume-based discounts, and consider multi-vendor bidding to restore competitive tension.
• Network Infrastructure Optimization- Evaluate opportunities such as tower and site sharing with other 
operators, energy-efficient equipment upgrades, and decommissioning of redundant or underutilized sites.
• Zero-Based Cost Framework- Apply a zero-based budgeting lens to non-network costs (customer service, 
back-office, real estate) to challenge legacy spend rather than trimming incrementally.
• Impact vs. Effort Prioritization- Plot identified initiatives on an impact-versus-effort matrix, sequencing 
quick wins (vendor renegotiation) ahead of longer-term structural changes (infrastructure sharing).
• Quality Safeguards- Define minimum service-quality thresholds (network uptime, call drop rates, data 
speeds) that must be protected throughout implementation, with monitoring built into each initiative.
Impact
• Improved Margins- Renegotiated vendor contracts and infrastructure efficiencies directly reduce the cost 
base and help offset ARPU decline.
• Structured Decision-Making- A repeatable cost framework replaces ad hoc cuts, giving leadership a 
consistent way to evaluate future cost initiatives.
• Protected Service Quality- Built-in quality safeguards ensure cost reduction does not come at the expense of 
customer experience or churn.
• Stronger Vendor Leverage- A systematic contract review process improves the operator's negotiating 
position on an ongoing basis, not just as a one-time exercise.
Final Note
Addressing margin pressure in telecom requires more than isolated cost cuts. By combining vendor renegotiation, 
infrastructure optimization, and a disciplined prioritization framework, the operator can protect service quality while 
building a sustainable, repeatable approach to cost management.

• How should the bank balance quick wins against longer-term platform investments?
• What role should data and personalization play in the bank's strategy to retain younger customers?

Case Study on Digital 
Transformation Roadmap
3. Digital Transformation Roadmap – Banking: How a mid-sized bank can compete with digital-
first fintechs and neo-banks.
Introduction
A mid-sized bank is losing younger customers to digital-first fintech competitors and neo-banks that offer seamless 
mobile experiences. This case study explores how the bank can design a digital transformation roadmap, prioritizing 
the right initiatives across a multi-year horizon.
Background
The bank has a loyal base of older customers built on branch relationships and traditional trust, but its digital 
initiatives have been fragmented across departments, with no unified strategy guiding investment. The mobile app is 
outdated relative to fintech competitors, offering limited functionality and a clunky user experience.
The bank also makes limited use of the customer data it already holds, missing opportunities for personalization that 
neo-banks use effectively to deepen engagement. As younger, digitally native customers increasingly choose fintech 
alternatives for everyday banking, the bank risks losing an entire generation of future customers.
Designing the Digital Transformation Roadmap
• Digital Maturity Assessment- Audit existing digital initiatives, technology stack, and customer journeys to 
identify gaps against leading fintech and neo-bank experiences.
• Unified Digital Strategy- Consolidate fragmented initiatives under a single roadmap with clear ownership, 
replacing siloed departmental efforts with a coordinated, bank-wide program.
• Core Mobile Experience Overhaul- Prioritize a rebuilt mobile app with essential, high-frequency features 
(instant transfers, spend tracking, simple onboarding) delivered early to stop customer attrition.
• Data-Driven Personalization- Invest in a customer data platform that unifies transaction and behavioral data 
to enable targeted offers, personalized product recommendations, and proactive service.
• Talent and Partnerships- Build internal digital product and engineering capability while selectively 
partnering with fintechs for capabilities that would take too long to build in-house.
• Phased Roadmap- Sequence initiatives across a three-year horizon, balancing quick, visible wins in year one 
with deeper platform and data investments by year three.
Impact
• Slowed Customer Attrition- A modernized mobile experience addresses the most visible gap driving 
younger customers to competitors.
• Improved Engagement- Data-driven personalization increases relevance of offers and products, deepening 
customer relationships over time.
• Coordinated Execution- A unified roadmap eliminates duplicated effort and ensures digital investment is 
directed toward the highest-impact initiatives.
• Long-Term Competitiveness- Building internal digital capability, supported by targeted partnerships, 
positions the bank to keep pace with fintech innovation beyond the initial roadmap.
Final Note
Competing with digital-first fintechs requires the bank to move beyond fragmented digital projects toward a 
coordinated, customer-centric transformation. By prioritizing a strong core mobile experience early and building 
toward deeper data and platform capabilities over three years, the bank can defend its customer base while laying the 
foundation for long-term digital competitiveness.
Questions for Discussion
• How would you design a digital transformation roadmap for this bank?
• What would you prioritize in year one versus year three?
• How should the bank balance quick wins against longer-term platform investments?
• What role should data and personalization play in the bank's strategy to retain younger customers?
