title: Case Study on Organizational Restructuring – Manufacturing
question:
• How can companies balance the need for aggressive cost synergies with the risk 
of damaging employee morale during a restructuring? 
• What specific metrics should leadership use to objectively evaluate candidates 
when deciding between two employees for a single consolidated role? 
• How does an undefined or poorly communicated operating model contribute to 
post-merger integration failure? 
• What role does transparent communication play in mitigating productivity loss 
during the uncertainty of an organizational redesign?
solution_approach:
Case Study on Organizational Restructuring – Manufacturing 
4. How a manufacturing company redesigned its organizational structure post-merger 
to resolve role overlaps and realize cost synergies. 
Introduction A prominent manufacturing company recently completed a major 
acquisition aimed at driving growth and market consolidation. However, the integration 
process resulted in overlapping departments, duplicated roles, and unclear reporting 
lines. This case study explores the organizational redesign strategy implemented to 
resolve these post-merger challenges, streamline operations, and capture intended 
financial benefits. 
Background Following the acquisition, the combined entity struggled with severe 
structural inefficiencies. The presence of redundant roles across the legacy and 
acquired companies led to intense role ambiguity. Consequently, the organization 
experienced slow decision-making, plummeting employee morale, and failed to realize 
the projected cost synergies from the merger, necessitating an immediate restructuring 
intervention. 
Restructuring Strategies 
• Operating Model Alignment: The company first defined the future-state 
operating model to ensure the new structure supported the combined entity's 
strategic goals. This involved centralizing shared services (like HR, Finance, and 
IT) to reduce redundancies, while decentralizing plant operations to maintain 
local agility. 
• Role Mapping and 'Spans and Layers' Framework: The organization applied a 
"Spans and Layers" framework to audit reporting lines. By mapping out 
overlapping roles, they aimed to widen the span of control (the number of direct 
reports per manager) and reduce unnecessary hierarchical layers to accelerate 
decision-making. 
• Competency and Skills Assessment (The "Best Fit" Approach): To resolve role 
overlaps objectively, the company utilized competency matrices and 
performance metrics. Employees in duplicated roles were evaluated based on 
future-state requirements, ensuring the most qualified individuals were retained 
or reassigned regardless of their legacy company affiliation. 
• Change Management and Transparent Communication: A robust 
communication plan was established to address employee anxieties. This 
included clear timelines for the restructuring, transparent criteria for role 
selection, and transition support/severance packages for displaced workers to 
protect the morale of the remaining staff. 
Impact 
• Accelerated Decision-Making: Streamlined reporting lines and reduced 
hierarchical layers eliminated bottlenecks, allowing for faster, more agile 
operational and strategic decisions. 
• Realized Cost Synergies: Consolidating overlapping departments and 
eliminating duplicated roles significantly reduced overhead costs, enabling the 
company to achieve the merger's financial targets. 
• Improved Employee Morale: Clear role definitions, transparent 
communication, and structured reporting lines removed ambiguity, restoring 
employee confidence and daily productivity. 
• Operational Efficiency: A unified operating model ensured that both legacy and 
acquired manufacturing units worked cohesively under a single, standardized 
framework. 
Final Note This restructuring initiative demonstrates that a successful merger extends 
beyond financial transactions into complex human capital and structural integration. By 
applying objective frameworks to resolve role overlaps and aligning the organization 
with a clear operating model, the manufacturing company successfully navigated post-
merger turbulence to unlock its true synergistic value. 
Questions for Discussion 
• How can companies balance the need for aggressive cost synergies with the risk 
of damaging employee morale during a restructuring? 
• What specific metrics should leadership use to objectively evaluate candidates 
when deciding between two employees for a single consolidated role? 
• How does an undefined or poorly communicated operating model contribute to 
post-merger integration failure? 
• What role does transparent communication play in mitigating productivity loss 
during the uncertainty of an organizational redesign?

Worth Asking First
Scope of the market — the entire India two-wheeler insurance industry (all insurers), or just the
addressable opportunity for one new entrant?
Type of cover — mandatory third-party (TP) only, or TP plus comprehensive/own-damage (OD)
policies combined?
Commercial fleets — are delivery-rider two-wheelers (Swiggy, Zomato, Amazon last-mile) in scope,
or personal-use vehicles only?
Flow vs. stock — GWP is this year's premium income (mostly renewals plus new policies), not the
total value of vehicles on the road. Worth stating out loud so the interviewer knows you know the
difference.
For  a  15-minute  guesstimate,  it's  fine  to  say:  "I'll  scope  this  to  personal-use  two-wheelers,  combine  TP  and
comprehensive, and treat EVs and petrol bikes together — happy to peel those apart if useful," and then just move.

Guesstimate Case Study · India Two-Wheeler Insurance · Page 2 of 7
Building the Number
1 Start with the base — how many two-wheelers are actually on the road
Not how many were sold this year. How many exist, full stop. India registers close to 2 crore new two-
wheelers a year now (1.89 crore in 2024, just over 2 crore in 2025), and has been doing so at scale for
over a decade. Government VAHAN data and independent trackers converge on a total operating parc
somewhere in the 26–30 crore range as of the mid-2020s.
Working assumption: ~28 crore two-wheelers on Indian roads today — the single largest two-
wheeler fleet of any country on earth. Nobody expects you to know this to the decimal; what they're
checking is whether your order of magnitude is sane and whether you can defend it if pushed.
2 Segment by engine capacity — not by geography
The instinct in most guesstimates is to split urban vs. rural first. Resist it here. The regulator itself (IRDAI)
prices third-party premiums by engine capacity band, and that band happens to correlate tightly with
income, financing behaviour, and — as you'll see in Step 3 — how likely someone is to actually keep their
insurance current. So segment on the variable the rest of your logic will hang off.

3 Apply insurance penetration — the step every generic casebook skips
This is the crux of the whole case. IRDAI's own data, echoed by a widely-cited General Insurance Council
survey, puts uninsured vehicles at roughly 55–60% of everything on Indian roads — and two-wheelers
make up the overwhelming majority of that uninsured pool. People buy a bike, insure it for the mandatory
long-term period at purchase, and then simply let the policy lapse at renewal. There's no roadside
enforcement mechanism that catches this at scale, so the leak just sits there.
Guesstimate Case Study · India Two-Wheeler Insurance · Page 3 of 7
REALITY CHECK
If you didn't know this stat walking in, you're not expected to. The move is to say out loud: "I'd
guess a meaningful share of two-wheelers are uninsured despite the legal mandate — say 30–
40% — because enforcement is weak and renewal reminders are easy to ignore." That's a
defensible assumption even without the exact number. Getting the direction right (penetration is
well under 100%) is what separates a strong answer from a forgettable one.
Penetration isn't uniform across segments either — cheaper, older bikes skew uninsured (low residual
value, cash-purchased, no lender forcing renewal); premium bikes skew insured (financed, higher owner
engagement, dealership push).

commercial-use risk higher) that a personal-use-only build simply excludes.
Comprehensive premiums were estimated conservatively. High-value scooters and electric two-
wheelers — with expensive battery packs to insure — carry own-damage premiums well above the
round numbers assumed here.

personal accident cover add-ons sit on top of every number in the table above.

What This Case Is Actually Testing
None of the interviewers asking this question care whether you land on ₹27,700 crore or ₹40,000 crore.
They're watching for four things:
MECE instinct. Did you split the market into buckets that don't overlap and cover the whole
population, before layering on an assumption — rather than assuming one blended number for 28
crore very different vehicles?
Willingness to challenge the "obvious" input. Most candidates silently assume 100% insurance
compliance because the vehicle physically exists. The stronger candidates ask whether that's even
true.
Comfort narrating uncertainty. Saying "I don't know the exact penetration rate, so I'll assume X and
flag it" out loud is worth more than guessing silently and hoping nobody probes.
Actually sanity-checking the output. Comparing your number to any real-world anchor — even a
rough one — and being able to explain a gap instead of being rattled by it.
COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID
Treating 28 crore two-wheelers as one monolithic block instead of segmenting by a variable that
changes behaviour.
Confusing GWP (a yearly flow of premium income) with the total value of vehicles on the road, or
with the number of policies sold.
Going silent when unsure of a number — narrate the logic even when the input is a rough guess.
Presenting the final number as precise. "Roughly ₹25,000–30,000 crore, and here's why" reads far
better than a suspiciously exact figure.
For whoever presents this to the batch: spend the first five minutes just on Step 3 — cold-calling a few people on
"what % of two-wheelers do you think are insured?" before revealing 55–60% uninsured tends to land the whole lesson
better than any amount of explanation afterward. Let the surprise do the teaching.

Blind Spot
Sizing India's motor insurance market when nearly half the
vehicles on the road aren't actually covered.

and-fridges problems.
Consulting Prep Series Guesstimate No. 6  ·  Insurance & Financial Services
Before You Start
Every guesstimate that's been passed around the batch so far has been about counting things that
visibly exist — cabs on a street, fridges in a home, credit cards in a wallet. This one is different. It's
about counting something that, for more than half the population in question, isn't actually there.
Insurance sizing questions have been turning up in first and second rounds more than they used
to, especially with boutique firms that work with NBFCs and insurers. It's a good test precisely
because the "obvious" version of the answer is wrong. Most people size this market by assuming
every registered vehicle carries a policy. It doesn't. Roughly 55–60% of two-wheelers in India ride
around without valid insurance at any given time, and that single fact changes the entire shape of
the estimate.

GUESSTIMATE CASE STUDY  ·  CONSULTING PREP LIBRARY
The Two-Wheeler
Blind Spot
Sizing India's motor insurance market when nearly half the
vehicles on the road aren't actually covered.
A new case for the guesstimate shelf — built because BFSI sizing
questions are showing up in first rounds more often than most prep
material accounts for, and none of them look like the standard cabs-
and-fridges problems.
Consulting Prep Series Guesstimate No. 6  ·  Insurance & Financial Services
Before You Start
Every guesstimate that's been passed around the batch so far has been about counting things that
visibly exist — cabs on a street, fridges in a home, credit cards in a wallet. This one is different. It's
about counting something that, for more than half the population in question, isn't actually there.
Insurance sizing questions have been turning up in first and second rounds more than they used
to, especially with boutique firms that work with NBFCs and insurers. It's a good test precisely
because the "obvious" version of the answer is wrong. Most people size this market by assuming
every registered vehicle carries a policy. It doesn't. Roughly 55–60% of two-wheelers in India ride
around without valid insurance at any given time, and that single fact changes the entire shape of
the estimate.
Work through this the same way you'd work through the operational-risk case on the metals
industry  already  in  the  folder:  segment  first  using  a  variable  that  actually  drives  different
behaviour, apply assumptions inside each segment instead of at the top, and then sanity-check the
output against whatever real number you can dig up — even a rough one. That habit matters more
than getting any single figure exactly right.
THE CASE PROMPT
"One of our clients is a digital-first general insurance company. They currently sell health and
travel cover, and they're deciding whether to enter two-wheeler insurance in India. Before we
commission full diligence, I want your back-of-the-envelope estimate of the annual Gross
Written Premium for two-wheeler insurance in India today. Talk me through your thinking as
you go."
You have a blank sheet, a pen, and roughly 15 minutes. No laptop, no search engine — just what you already
know or can reasonably assume.
Q Clarifying Questions Worth Asking First
Scope of the market — the entire India two-wheeler insurance industry (all insurers), or just the
addressable opportunity for one new entrant?
Type of cover — mandatory third-party (TP) only, or TP plus comprehensive/own-damage (OD)
policies combined?
Commercial fleets — are delivery-rider two-wheelers (Swiggy, Zomato, Amazon last-mile) in scope,
or personal-use vehicles only?
Flow vs. stock — GWP is this year's premium income (mostly renewals plus new policies), not the
total value of vehicles on the road. Worth stating out loud so the interviewer knows you know the
difference.
For  a  15-minute  guesstimate,  it's  fine  to  say:  "I'll  scope  this  to  personal-use  two-wheelers,  combine  TP  and
comprehensive, and treat EVs and petrol bikes together — happy to peel those apart if useful," and then just move.

Building the Number
1 Start with the base — how many two-wheelers are actually on the road
Not how many were sold this year. How many exist, full stop. India registers close to 2 crore new two-
wheelers a year now (1.89 crore in 2024, just over 2 crore in 2025), and has been doing so at scale for
over a decade. Government VAHAN data and independent trackers converge on a total operating parc
somewhere in the 26–30 crore range as of the mid-2020s.
Working assumption: ~28 crore two-wheelers on Indian roads today — the single largest two-
wheeler fleet of any country on earth. Nobody expects you to know this to the decimal; what they're
checking is whether your order of magnitude is sane and whether you can defend it if pushed.
2 Segment by engine capacity — not by geography
The instinct in most guesstimates is to split urban vs. rural first. Resist it here. The regulator itself (IRDAI)
prices third-party premiums by engine capacity band, and that band happens to correlate tightly with
income, financing behaviour, and — as you'll see in Step 3 — how likely someone is to actually keep their
insurance current. So segment on the variable the rest of your logic will hang off.

3 Apply insurance penetration — the step every generic casebook skips
This is the crux of the whole case. IRDAI's own data, echoed by a widely-cited General Insurance Council
survey, puts uninsured vehicles at roughly 55–60% of everything on Indian roads — and two-wheelers
make up the overwhelming majority of that uninsured pool. People buy a bike, insure it for the mandatory

enforcement mechanism that catches this at scale, so the leak just sits there.

title: Consulting Project Volume – Management Consulting Firm
question: Walk through your step-by-step approach to solve: Consulting Project Volume – Management Consulting Firm. Clearly state your assumptions, drivers, and final estimate.
solution_approach:
Consulting Project Volume – Management Consulting Firm
Context: A top-tier management consulting firm has an India office with 500 consultants (Associates to 
Partners).
Estimate the number of client projects this office would execute in a year. Also estimate the average 
revenue generated per project.
Let us first think about how the 500 consultants are deployed across projects. A typical top-tier 
engagement team is staffed across the pyramid — a fractional Partner, a Principal or Engagement 
Manager, a couple of Consultants, and a couple of Associates. Assume an average project team size of 
about 6 consultants, blending junior and senior staff.
Not every week in the year is billable. Consultants take vacation, attend training, do internal staffing and 
business development, and spend some time on the bench between projects. Assume about 46 billable 
weeks per consultant per year out of 52.
This gives a total capacity of 500 × 46 = 23,000 consultant-weeks available across the office in a year.
Next, consider how long a typical engagement runs. Strategy and operations projects at a top-tier firm 
usually run for about 10 to 12 weeks; assume 12 weeks as the average. Each project therefore consumes 
about 6 × 12 = 72 consultant-weeks of capacity.
Number of projects per year = total consultant-weeks available ÷ consultant-weeks per project = 23,000 ÷ 
72 ≈ 320 projects per year.
Now let us estimate average revenue per project. Billing rates at a top-tier firm's India office are blended 
across the pyramid — Associates bill lower and Partners bill much higher — so assume an average 
blended rate of about USD 9,000 per consultant per week.
Average revenue per project = team size × duration × weekly billing rate = 6 × 12 × USD 9,000 ≈ USD 
650,000.
As a sanity check, multiplying projects per year by average revenue per project gives 320 × USD 650,000 
≈ USD 208 million in annual office revenue, or roughly USD 415,000 of revenue per consultant per year 
— a reasonable figure for a top-tier firm's India practice.
So, a good final guesstimate is that the India office executes about 300 to 320 client projects per year, at 
an average revenue of roughly USD 600,000 to 700,000 per project.

title: Management Consulting Market Size – India
question: Walk through your step-by-step approach to solve: Management Consulting Market Size – India. Clearly state your assumptions, drivers, and final estimate.
solution_approach:
Management Consulting Market Size – India
Context: Indian companies across sectors increasingly hire consulting firms for strategy, operations, and 
digital transformation projects.
Estimate the total annual market size (in USD) of the management consulting industry in India. 
Structure your approach by client segments (large enterprises, mid-size, PE-backed firms) and 
typical spend per engagement.
Let us first estimate the universe of companies in India that are large enough to hire management 
consultants for strategy, operations, and digital transformation work. We can segment this into three 
buyer groups: large enterprises, mid-size companies, and PE-backed firms. Assume there are about 5,000 
large enterprises (revenue above roughly USD 500 million), 50,000 mid-size enterprises (revenue 
between USD 50 million and USD 500 million), and 2,000 PE-backed portfolio companies actively 
working to professionalize operations ahead of an exit.
Not every company in these segments hires a consulting firm every year. Large enterprises regularly run 
strategy and transformation projects, so assume an annual engagement rate of about 25 percent. Mid-size 
companies are more selective and price-sensitive, so assume a lower engagement rate of about 8 percent. 
PE-backed firms, on the other hand, are frequently pushed by their investors to bring in consultants for 
value-creation and operational improvement plans, so assume a higher engagement rate of about 40 
percent.
Typical spend per engagement also varies by segment. Large enterprises can afford large, multi-month 
strategy or digital transformation engagements, averaging about USD 800,000 per project. Mid-size 
companies typically commission smaller, more focused engagements averaging about USD 150,000. PE-
backed firms tend to run tightly scoped, high-intensity value-creation projects averaging about USD 
300,000.
Using this, the annual market can be estimated as follows:
Large enterprises: 5,000 × 25 percent × USD 800,000 = USD 1.0 billion.
Mid-size enterprises: 50,000 × 8 percent × USD 150,000 = USD 600 million.
PE-backed firms: 2,000 × 40 percent × USD 300,000 = USD 240 million.
Adding these, the base management consulting market comes to about USD 1.84 billion.
However, many engagements extend beyond the core strategy scope into implementation support, digital 
and technology advisory, and change management, which can add meaningfully to overall spend. If these 
adjacent services increase realized revenue by roughly 40 to 50 percent, the market can reasonably be 
estimated at around USD 2.5 to 2.8 billion annually.
So, a good final guesstimate is that the annual management consulting market in India is about USD 2.6 
billion, with a reasonable range of USD 2.3 to 2.9 billion.

Number of Credit Cards in India 
 
Guesstimate Problem Statement 
Estimate the total number of credit cards in India. 
As a consultant, you are required to estimate the total number of credit cards held by Indians without using 
external data sources. Use logical assumptions, population segmentation by income group, willingness to take 
on credit, and loan-application behaviour to arrive at an approximate estimate. 
 
Step-by-Step Solution 
Step 1: Start with India's Population 
Assume: 
Population of India = 1.4 Billion 
Step 2: Segment Population by Income Group 
Assumption: India is a low-to-middle income earning country, hence a relatively small share of the 
population falls in the high-income bracket.

High Income 10% 140 Million 
Medium Income 60% 840 Million 
Low Income 30% 420 Million 
Step 3: Estimate the Earning Population within Each Group 
Assumption: The percentage of working individuals (including working women) is higher in the high- and 
low-income categories compared to the middle-income category, where a larger share is dependent/non-
earning. 
Income Group % Earning People Earning 
High Income 100% 140 Million 
Medium Income 50% 420 Million 
Low Income 100% 420 Million 
Step 4: Estimate Willingness for Credit/Loan 
Assumption: Low-income earners tend to prefer informal loans over formal credit instruments like credit 
cards, while middle-income earners represent a growing population with increasing credit needs. 
Income Group % Willing Population Willing 
High Income 50% 70 Million 
Medium Income 30% 126 Million 
Low Income 10% 42 Million 
Step 5: Estimate the Population Actually Applying for Credit Cards 
Assumption: Not everyone willing to take credit ends up applying – approval likelihood and awareness of the 
product differ by income group. 
Income Group % Actually Applying Population Applying 
High Income 70% 50 Million 
Medium Income 40% 50 Million 
Low Income 20% 10 Million 
Step 6: Apply Average Number of Credit Cards Held per Person 
Assumption: Higher-income individuals are more likely to hold multiple credit cards (e.g., for rewards, travel, 
or business use), while middle- and low-income cardholders typically hold just one. 
Income Group Avg. Cards per Person Total Credit Cards 
High Income 2 50M × 2 = 100 Million 
Medium Income 1 50M × 1 = 50 Million 
Low Income 1 10M × 1 = 10 Million 
Step 7: Arrive at Final Estimate 
Total Credit Cards = 100 Million + 50 Million + 10 Million 
Total Number of Credit Cards in India 
≈ 160 Million Credit Cards 
 
Final Answer 
Estimated total number of credit cards in India ≈ 160 Million. 
 
Consulting Interview Takeaway 
The interviewer is not evaluating whether the answer is exactly correct. They are evaluating: 
● Structured Thinking – Did the candidate break the problem logically from population down to actual 
cardholders? 
● MECE Segmentation – Were income-group buckets mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive? 
● Reasonable Assumptions – Are the earning %, willingness, and application-rate assumptions 
defendable and internally consistent? 
● Mental Math Accuracy – Can the candidate calculate quickly and correctly across multiple funnel 
layers? 
● Business Logic – Did the candidate connect income level, financial behaviour, and product-holding 
patterns (multiple cards for high income) to reach the estimate? 
A concise consulting framework for this guesstimate would be: 
Population → Income Segmentation → Earning Population → Willingness for Credit → Actual Applications 
→ Avg. Cards per Person → Total Credit Cards

title: IT Helpdesk Ticket Volume – ITES
question: Walk through your step-by-step approach to solve: IT Helpdesk Ticket Volume – ITES. Clearly state your assumptions, drivers, and final estimate.
solution_approach:
IT Helpdesk Ticket Volume – ITES
Context: A large IT services company has 50,000 employees across India, all using company-issued 
laptops and enterprise software (email, VPN, ERP, etc.).
Estimate the number of IT helpdesk tickets (hardware + software issues) raised annually across this 
organization. Also estimate how many support agents would be needed to handle this volume.
Let us first break down the ticket volume by issue type, since employees raise tickets at different rates 
depending on the category of problem. We can split this into three buckets: hardware issues (laptop 
malfunctions, peripherals), software issues (application errors, ERP problems, installations), and access or 
network issues (email, VPN, password resets).
Assume hardware issues occur at about 0.3 tickets per employee per month, software issues at about 0.6 
tickets per employee per month, and access or network issues at about 0.6 tickets per employee per 
month, giving a blended rate of about 1.5 tickets per employee per month.
Using this, the annual ticket volume can be estimated as follows:
Hardware issues: 50,000 × 0.3 × 12 = 180,000 tickets.
Software issues: 50,000 × 0.6 × 12 = 360,000 tickets.
Access/network issues: 50,000 × 0.6 × 12 = 360,000 tickets.
Adding these, the organization raises about 900,000 helpdesk tickets annually.
Now let us estimate the number of support agents needed to handle this volume. Assume an agent works 
an 8-hour day, but after breaks, internal meetings, and non-ticket work, only about 80 percent of that time 
(roughly 384 minutes) is spent actively resolving tickets.
Assume an average handling time of about 20 minutes per ticket (mixing quick password resets with 
longer hardware troubleshooting). That gives about 384 ÷ 20 ≈ 19 tickets resolved per agent per day.
Assuming an agent works about 250 days a year after accounting for weekends, holidays, and leave, each 
agent can resolve about 19 × 250 ≈ 4,750 tickets per year.
Number of agents required = total annual tickets ÷ tickets handled per agent per year = 900,000 ÷ 4,750 ≈ 
190 agents.

IT Helpdesk Ticket Volume – ITES
Context: A large IT services company has 50,000 employees across India, all using company-issued 
laptops and enterprise software (email, VPN, ERP, etc.).
Estimate the number of IT helpdesk tickets (hardware + software issues) raised annually across this 
organization. Also estimate how many support agents would be needed to handle this volume.
Let us first break down the ticket volume by issue type, since employees raise tickets at different rates 
depending on the category of problem. We can split this into three buckets: hardware issues (laptop 
malfunctions, peripherals), software issues (application errors, ERP problems, installations), and access or 
network issues (email, VPN, password resets).
Assume hardware issues occur at about 0.3 tickets per employee per month, software issues at about 0.6 
tickets per employee per month, and access or network issues at about 0.6 tickets per employee per 
month, giving a blended rate of about 1.5 tickets per employee per month.
Using this, the annual ticket volume can be estimated as follows:
Hardware issues: 50,000 × 0.3 × 12 = 180,000 tickets.
Software issues: 50,000 × 0.6 × 12 = 360,000 tickets.
Access/network issues: 50,000 × 0.6 × 12 = 360,000 tickets.
Adding these, the organization raises about 900,000 helpdesk tickets annually.
Now let us estimate the number of support agents needed to handle this volume. Assume an agent works 
an 8-hour day, but after breaks, internal meetings, and non-ticket work, only about 80 percent of that time 
(roughly 384 minutes) is spent actively resolving tickets.
Assume an average handling time of about 20 minutes per ticket (mixing quick password resets with 
longer hardware troubleshooting). That gives about 384 ÷ 20 ≈ 19 tickets resolved per agent per day.
Assuming an agent works about 250 days a year after accounting for weekends, holidays, and leave, each 
agent can resolve about 19 × 250 ≈ 4,750 tickets per year.
Number of agents required = total annual tickets ÷ tickets handled per agent per year = 900,000 ÷ 4,750 ≈ 
190 agents.
Adding a small buffer for shift overlap, escalations to tier-2 support, and team leads, a reasonable 
estimate is about 190 to 210 support agents.
So, a good final guesstimate is that the organization raises about 900,000 IT helpdesk tickets annually, 
requiring roughly 200 support agents to handle the volume.

title: Cloud Migration Market Size – IT Services
question: Walk through your step-by-step approach to solve: Cloud Migration Market Size – IT Services. Clearly state your assumptions, drivers, and final estimate.
solution_approach:
Cloud Migration Market Size – IT Services 
 
Context: Indian enterprises across sectors (BFSI, retail, manufacturing) are increasingly migrating 
their on-premise IT infrastructure to the cloud. 
 
Estimate the annual market size (in USD) of the cloud migration services industry in India. 
Break down your assumptions by company size, sector adoption rate, and average deal value. 
 
First, let us consider the number of enterprises in India across BFSI, retail, and 
manufacturing that are relevant for cloud migration services. Assume there are around 
5,000 large enterprises, 50,000 mid-sized enterprises, and 200,000 small enterprises. That 
gives a total base of about 255,000 companies.  
Now assume that only a fraction of these companies will undertake cloud migration in a 
given year. Since BFSI, retail, and manufacturing are actively digitizing, a reasonable 
blended annual migration rate would be about 9 percent. That means around 23,000 
companies migrate to the cloud each year.  
The deal size depends on company size. Assume a large enterprise migration project is 
worth about USD 500,000, a mid-sized company project is worth about USD 100,000, and 
a small company project is worth about USD 20,000.  
Using this, the annual market can be estimated as follows: 
Large enterprises: 5,000 × 15 percent × USD 500,000 = USD 375 million.  
Mid-sized enterprises: 50,000 × 10 percent × USD 100,000 = USD 500 million.  
Small enterprises: 200,000 × 8.6 percent × USD 20,000 = USD 344 million.  
Adding these, the base migration market comes to about USD 1.2 billion. 
However, cloud migration projects often include adjacent services such as architecture 
redesign, security setup, data migration, and post-migration support. If these increase 
project value meaningfully, the market can reasonably be estimated at around USD 2 to 2.8 
billion annually.  
So, a good final guesstimate is that the annual cloud migration services market in India is 
about USD 2.5 billion, with a reasonable range of USD 2 to 2.8 billion.

title: Guesstimate 01: NovaTel's 5G Market Opportunity
question: Walk through your step-by-step approach to solve: Guesstimate 01: NovaTel's 5G Market Opportunity. Clearly state your assumptions, drivers, and final estimate.
solution_approach:
Guesstimate 01: NovaTel's 5G Market Opportunity
Domain: Sales and Marketing
Problem Statement
NovaTel Communications is planning to launch a premium 5G plan in Pune. Before investing in a
large marketing campaign, the management wants to estimate the potential market.
Question
Estimate the number of customers in Pune who would subscribe to a premium 5G plan within the
first year.
Concepts Tested
 Market Sizing
 Segmentation
 Consumer Behaviour
 Adoption Rates
 Assumption Building

How many customers will subscribe to NovaTel's
 premium 5G plan in Pune during the first year?
First, let's estimate the population of Pune. Assume Pune has around 8 million residents.
Assume that about 70% are adults who make their own telecom purchasing decisions. This gives
roughly 5.6 million adults.
Not everyone owns a smartphone. Assume smartphone penetration is about 85%, resulting in
approximately 4.8 million smartphone users.
Since the plan is a premium 5G plan, only users with 5G-capable devices are relevant. Assume
45% own compatible phones, giving around 2.2 million users.
Premium plans generally appeal to higher-income or heavy-data users. Assume 30% belong to this
segment, leaving about 660,000 potential customers.
NovaTel will face competition from existing telecom operators. Assume it captures 25% of this
premium segment during its launch year, giving roughly 165,000 customers.
Not everyone will adopt immediately. Assuming a first-year adoption rate of 35%, the estimated
subscribers become approximately 58,000.
Therefore, we estimate that NovaTel could acquire around 60,000 premium 5G subscribers in Pune
during its first year.

question: Walk through your step-by-step approach to solve: Guesstimate 02: SwiftKart Dark Store Expansion. Clearly state your assumptions, drivers, and final estimate.
solution_approach:
Guesstimate 02: SwiftKart Dark Store Expansion
Domain: Sales and Marketing
Problem Statement
SwiftKart is considering opening a new dark store in Jaipur.
Question
Estimate the number of daily orders required for the store to break even within one year.
Students May Consider
 Population
 Order Frequency
 Delivery Radius
 Average Order Value
 Contribution Margin
 Fixed Operating Costs
Concepts Tested
 Unit Economics
 Break-even Analysis
 Market Demand
 Profitability

How many daily orders does a SwiftKart dark store
 need to break even within one year?
First, estimate the annual operating cost of one dark store. Assume fixed costs (rent, salaries,
utilities and technology) total around ■3.6 crore per year.
Next, estimate the average order value. Assume customers spend ■600 per order.
Dark stores earn only the contribution margin after variable costs. Assume the contribution margin
is 20%, giving ■120 contribution per order.
To recover ■3.6 crore annually, the store must complete ■3.6 crore ÷ ■120 ≈ 300,000 orders each
year.
Dividing by 365 days gives approximately 822 orders per day.
Rounding up to provide a safety buffer, the store should target about 850 daily orders to
comfortably break even.

title: Estimating the Annual Sale of Domestic Refrigerators in India
question: Walk through your step-by-step approach to solve: Estimating the Annual Sale of Domestic Refrigerators in India. Clearly state your assumptions, drivers, and final estimate.
solution_approach:
Guesstimate Case Study 
Estimating the Annual Sale of Domestic Refrigerators in India 
1. Problem Statement 
Estimate the number of refrigerators sold in India every year. 
2. Clarifying Question 
Interviewee: Should we consider domestic refrigerators only, or include commercial 
refrigerators too? 
Interviewer: For this question, consider only domestic refrigerators. 
3. Approach 
Approach used: Demand-Side (Top-Down) Approach 
Guesstimates like this can typically be solved using a demand-side approach (estimating end-
consumer need and working down to units), a supply-side approach (estimating from 
manufacturer/dealer production and sales data), or a bottom-up approach (building up from a 
small, known unit and scaling). This solution uses the demand-side approach — first 
estimating the total addressable market (i.e., total refrigerators currently owned across Indian 
households) by working top-down from population, and then converting this stock figure into 
annual unit sales by accounting for replacement demand and new/growth demand. 
● Why demand-side: household and income-class data (population, family size, income 
distribution) is more reliable to assume than manufacturer shipment data, making it 
the natural default for consumer durables like refrigerators. 
4. Step 1: Total Households in India 
Parameter Value 
Total population of India 130 crore 
Average family size 4 members 
Total households 130 / 4 = 32.5 crore 
5. Step 2: Segmenting Households 
Households are split by geography (Metro/Tier I, Tier II/III, and Villages), and within each 
geography, by income class (Poor, Middle-class, Rich). 
Segment Poor % Middle-class % Rich % 
Metro / Tier I 20% 60% 20% 
Tier II / III 40% 50% 10% 
Villages 60% 38% 2% 
Assumption on household split across geographies: Metro/Tier I = 20% of households, Tier 
II/III = 15%, and Villages = 65%. 
6. Step 3: Refrigerator Penetration Rate 
Penetration reflects the assumption that poor households do not own refrigerators, while 
ownership varies for middle-class and rich households by geography. 
Segment Poor Middle-class Rich 
Metro / Tier I 0% 50% 100% 
Tier II / III 0% 40% 100% 
Villages 0% 0% 100% 
7. Step 4: Market Size Calculation 
Segment Households (crore) Effective 
Penetration Refrigerators (crore) 
Metro / Tier I 0.20 × 32.5 = 6.50 50% 3.25 
Tier II / III 0.15 × 32.5 ≈ 5.00 30% 1.50 
Villages 0.65 × 32.5 ≈ 21.00 2% 0.42 
Total Market Size (Refrigerator Stock) = 3.25 + 1.50 + 0.42 ≈ 5.17 crore refrigerators 
8. Step 5: Converting Market Size to Annual Sales 
Annual unit sales are not the same as total market size. Two demand components drive yearly 
sales: 
● Replacement demand — households replacing an existing refrigerator that has 
reached the end of its useful life. 
● New / growth demand — first-time buyers, driven by rising incomes and household 
formation. 
Assumption Value 
Average life of a refrigerator 10 years 
Annual market growth rate 5% 
Formula 
Refrigerators sold per year = (Market size ÷ Average life) + (Growth rate × Market size) 
9. Final Calculation 
Component Calculation Value (crore) 
Replacement demand 5.17 / 10 0.517 
New / growth demand 5.17 × 0.05 0.259 
Total annual sales 0.517 + 0.259 ≈ 0.775 
Estimated refrigerators sold in India every year ≈ 0.775 crore ≈ 77.5 lakh units 
 
10. Key Takeaways for Presentation 
● Always begin by clarifying scope (domestic vs. commercial) before diving into 
numbers. 
● Explicitly name the approach (demand-side / supply-side / bottom-up) before starting 
the calculation — it signals structured thinking to the interviewer. 
● Structure the estimate top-down: Population → Households → Segments → 
Penetration → Market size. 
● Clearly separate 'market size' (stock) from 'annual sales' (flow) — this distinction is 
often what interviewers probe on. 
● State every assumption explicitly (family size, growth rate, product life) so the 
interviewer can challenge or adjust them. 
● Round numbers at each step to keep the mental math fast and the story easy to follow.

Background: Brands increasingly allocate advertising budgets to digital channels (Google, Meta, programmatic display, video).
Questions for Discussion
- Estimate the annual digital advertising market size (in INR) in India.
Approach:
1. Total active internet users in India (roughly 800 million).
2. Segment by daily active users (DAUs) who engage with ads: Urban high-intent (150 million), Tier 2/3 (350 million), Rural/low-intent (300 million).
3. Average digital ad spend per user per year (ARPU equivalent for ads): Urban (INR 1,200), Tier 2/3 (INR 400), Rural (INR 50).
4. Aggregating the segments: (150M * 1200) + (350M * 400) + (300M * 50) = 18,000 Cr + 14,000 Cr + 1,500 Cr = INR 33,500 Crore.
5. Cross-check against total ad spend in India (usually around 1 Lakh Crore, where digital is roughly 35-40%). This validates the estimate.

title: GUESSTIMATE CASE STUDY · CONSULTING PREP LIBRARY
question:
Worth Asking First
Scope of the market — the entire India two-wheeler insurance industry (all insurers), or just the
addressable opportunity for one new entrant?
Type of cover — mandatory third-party (TP) only, or TP plus comprehensive/own-damage (OD)
policies combined?
Commercial fleets — are delivery-rider two-wheelers (Swiggy, Zomato, Amazon last-mile) in scope,
or personal-use vehicles only?
Flow vs. stock — GWP is this year's premium income (mostly renewals plus new policies), not the
total value of vehicles on the road. Worth stating out loud so the interviewer knows you know the
difference.
For  a  15-minute  guesstimate,  it's  fine  to  say:  "I'll  scope  this  to  personal-use  two-wheelers,  combine  TP  and
comprehensive, and treat EVs and petrol bikes together — happy to peel those apart if useful," and then just move.
• 
• 
• 
• 
Guesstimate Case Study · India Two-Wheeler Insurance · Page 2 of 7
Building the Number
1 Start with the base — how many two-wheelers are actually on the road
Not how many were sold this year. How many exist, full stop. India registers close to 2 crore new two-
wheelers a year now (1.89 crore in 2024, just over 2 crore in 2025), and has been doing so at scale for
over a decade. Government VAHAN data and independent trackers converge on a total operating parc
somewhere in the 26–30 crore range as of the mid-2020s.
Working assumption: ~28 crore two-wheelers on Indian roads today — the single largest two-
wheeler fleet of any country on earth. Nobody expects you to know this to the decimal; what they're
checking is whether your order of magnitude is sane and whether you can defend it if pushed.
2 Segment by engine capacity — not by geography
The instinct in most guesstimates is to split urban vs. rural first. Resist it here. The regulator itself (IRDAI)
prices third-party premiums by engine capacity band, and that band happens to correlate tightly with
income, financing behaviour, and — as you'll see in Step 3 — how likely someone is to actually keep their
insurance current. So segment on the variable the rest of your logic will hang off.

These shares are a defensible guess based on how India's two-wheeler market is known to be dominated by sub-150cc
commuter bikes — not a cited statistic. Say so if asked.
3 Apply insurance penetration — the step every generic casebook skips
This is the crux of the whole case. IRDAI's own data, echoed by a widely-cited General Insurance Council
survey, puts uninsured vehicles at roughly 55–60% of everything on Indian roads — and two-wheelers
make up the overwhelming majority of that uninsured pool. People buy a bike, insure it for the mandatory
long-term period at purchase, and then simply let the policy lapse at renewal. There's no roadside
enforcement mechanism that catches this at scale, so the leak just sits there.
Guesstimate Case Study · India Two-Wheeler Insurance · Page 3 of 7
REALITY CHECK
If you didn't know this stat walking in, you're not expected to. The move is to say out loud: "I'd
guess a meaningful share of two-wheelers are uninsured despite the legal mandate — say 30–
40% — because enforcement is weak and renewal reminders are easy to ignore." That's a
defensible assumption even without the exact number. Getting the direction right (penetration is
well under 100%) is what separates a strong answer from a forgettable one.
Penetration isn't uniform across segments either — cheaper, older bikes skew uninsured (low residual
value, cash-purchased, no lender forcing renewal); premium bikes skew insured (financed, higher owner
engagement, dealership push).

75–150cc 21.84 40% 8.74
150–350cc 4.20 65% 2.73
>350cc 0.56 90% 0.50
Total 28.00 44% blended 12.32
Fig. 1 — The gap is concentrated in the mass commuter segment, in both absolute and relative terms.
4 Split third-party-only vs. comprehensive, then apply premiums
Within the insured base, owners either buy the cheapest legally-compliant option (third-party only, price
fixed annually by IRDAI) or a full comprehensive/package policy that also covers their own vehicle. That

split should tilt toward comprehensive as vehicle value climbs — nobody buys a bare third-party policy on
a ₹3 lakh superbike they financed on EMI.

5 Add it up

6 Sanity check — the step that actually earns the "hire"
A guesstimate nobody checks against reality is just arithmetic performed out loud. Industry research
(Mordor Intelligence and comparable trackers) sizes the actual India two-wheeler insurance market at
roughly US$5.66 billion in 2025 — about ₹47,300 crore. Our bottom-up build lands at 59% of that: right
order of magnitude, running low by around ₹19,500 crore.
Guesstimate Case Study · India Two-Wheeler Insurance · Page 5 of 7
Fig. 2 — Directionally right, materially short. That gap is the interesting part of the answer.
That shortfall isn't a failure — it's the most useful sentence you can say in the room. Three plausible
reasons, out loud, in order of likely weight:
Commercial and gig-economy fleets weren't modelled at all. Food-delivery and last-mile e-
commerce two-wheelers are a large, fast-growing, higher-premium segment (insurers price fleet and
commercial-use risk higher) that a personal-use-only build simply excludes.
Comprehensive premiums were estimated conservatively. High-value scooters and electric two-
wheelers — with expensive battery packs to insure — carry own-damage premiums well above the
round numbers assumed here.
GST and mandatory add-ons inflate written premium beyond the base policy price: 18% GST plus
personal accident cover add-ons sit on top of every number in the table above.

Guesstimate Case Study · India Two-Wheeler Insurance · Page 6 of 7
What This Case Is Actually Testing
None of the interviewers asking this question care whether you land on ₹27,700 crore or ₹40,000 crore.
They're watching for four things:
MECE instinct. Did you split the market into buckets that don't overlap and cover the whole
population, before layering on an assumption — rather than assuming one blended number for 28
crore very different vehicles?
Willingness to challenge the "obvious" input. Most candidates silently assume 100% insurance
compliance because the vehicle physically exists. The stronger candidates ask whether that's even
true.
Comfort narrating uncertainty. Saying "I don't know the exact penetration rate, so I'll assume X and
flag it" out loud is worth more than guessing silently and hoping nobody probes.
Actually sanity-checking the output. Comparing your number to any real-world anchor — even a
rough one — and being able to explain a gap instead of being rattled by it.
COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID
Treating 28 crore two-wheelers as one monolithic block instead of segmenting by a variable that
changes behaviour.
Confusing GWP (a yearly flow of premium income) with the total value of vehicles on the road, or
with the number of policies sold.
Going silent when unsure of a number — narrate the logic even when the input is a rough guess.
Presenting the final number as precise. "Roughly ₹25,000–30,000 crore, and here's why" reads far
better than a suspiciously exact figure.
For whoever presents this to the batch: spend the first five minutes just on Step 3 — cold-calling a few people on
"what % of two-wheelers do you think are insured?" before revealing 55–60% uninsured tends to land the whole lesson
better than any amount of explanation afterward. Let the surprise do the teaching.
— Consulting Prep Library, Guesstimate Series

Type of cover — mandatory third-party (TP) only, or TP plus comprehensive/own-damage (OD)
policies combined?
Commercial fleets — are delivery-rider two-wheelers (Swiggy, Zomato, Amazon last-mile) in scope,
or personal-use vehicles only?
Flow vs. stock — GWP is this year's premium income (mostly renewals plus new policies), not the
total value of vehicles on the road. Worth stating out loud so the interviewer knows you know the
difference.
For  a  15-minute  guesstimate,  it's  fine  to  say:  "I'll  scope  this  to  personal-use  two-wheelers,  combine  TP  and
comprehensive, and treat EVs and petrol bikes together — happy to peel those apart if useful," and then just move.

Building the Number
1 Start with the base — how many two-wheelers are actually on the road
Not how many were sold this year. How many exist, full stop. India registers close to 2 crore new two-
wheelers a year now (1.89 crore in 2024, just over 2 crore in 2025), and has been doing so at scale for
over a decade. Government VAHAN data and independent trackers converge on a total operating parc
somewhere in the 26–30 crore range as of the mid-2020s.
Working assumption: ~28 crore two-wheelers on Indian roads today — the single largest two-
wheeler fleet of any country on earth. Nobody expects you to know this to the decimal; what they're
checking is whether your order of magnitude is sane and whether you can defend it if pushed.
2 Segment by engine capacity — not by geography
The instinct in most guesstimates is to split urban vs. rural first. Resist it here. The regulator itself (IRDAI)
prices third-party premiums by engine capacity band, and that band happens to correlate tightly with
income, financing behaviour, and — as you'll see in Step 3 — how likely someone is to actually keep their
insurance current. So segment on the variable the rest of your logic will hang off.

3 Apply insurance penetration — the step every generic casebook skips
This is the crux of the whole case. IRDAI's own data, echoed by a widely-cited General Insurance Council
survey, puts uninsured vehicles at roughly 55–60% of everything on Indian roads — and two-wheelers
make up the overwhelming majority of that uninsured pool. People buy a bike, insure it for the mandatory
long-term period at purchase, and then simply let the policy lapse at renewal. There's no roadside
enforcement mechanism that catches this at scale, so the leak just sits there.

If you didn't know this stat walking in, you're not expected to. The move is to say out loud: "I'd

Penetration isn't uniform across segments either — cheaper, older bikes skew uninsured (low residual
value, cash-purchased, no lender forcing renewal); premium bikes skew insured (financed, higher owner
engagement, dealership push).

What This Case Is Actually Testing
None of the interviewers asking this question care whether you land on ₹27,700 crore or ₹40,000 crore.
They're watching for four things:
MECE instinct. Did you split the market into buckets that don't overlap and cover the whole
population, before layering on an assumption — rather than assuming one blended number for 28
crore very different vehicles?
Willingness to challenge the "obvious" input. Most candidates silently assume 100% insurance
compliance because the vehicle physically exists. The stronger candidates ask whether that's even
true.
Comfort narrating uncertainty. Saying "I don't know the exact penetration rate, so I'll assume X and
flag it" out loud is worth more than guessing silently and hoping nobody probes.
Actually sanity-checking the output. Comparing your number to any real-world anchor — even a
rough one — and being able to explain a gap instead of being rattled by it.
COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID
Treating 28 crore two-wheelers as one monolithic block instead of segmenting by a variable that
changes behaviour.
Confusing GWP (a yearly flow of premium income) with the total value of vehicles on the road, or
with the number of policies sold.
Going silent when unsure of a number — narrate the logic even when the input is a rough guess.
Presenting the final number as precise. "Roughly ₹25,000–30,000 crore, and here's why" reads far
better than a suspiciously exact figure.
For whoever presents this to the batch: spend the first five minutes just on Step 3 — cold-calling a few people on
"what % of two-wheelers do you think are insured?" before revealing 55–60% uninsured tends to land the whole lesson
better than any amount of explanation afterward. Let the surprise do the teaching.

title: Guesstimate: Digital Advertising Market Size in India
question:
- Estimate the annual digital advertising market size (in INR) in India.
Approach:
1. Total active internet users in India (roughly 800 million).
2. Segment by daily active users (DAUs) who engage with ads: Urban high-intent (150 million), Tier 2/3 (350 million), Rural/low-intent (300 million).
3. Average digital ad spend per user per year (ARPU equivalent for ads): Urban (INR 1,200), Tier 2/3 (INR 400), Rural (INR 50).
4. Aggregating the segments: (150M * 1200) + (350M * 400) + (300M * 50) = 18,000 Cr + 14,000 Cr + 1,500 Cr = INR 33,500 Crore.
5. Cross-check against total ad spend in India (usually around 1 Lakh Crore, where digital is roughly 35-40%). This validates the estimate.

title: Legacy System Modernization – Banking (BFSI)
question:
• Why is phased migration better than a full replacement for banks?  
• How does the strangler approach reduce operational risk?  
• What role does an API layer play in legacy modernization?  
• How can banks balance modernization with regulatory compliance?
solution_approach:
Legacy System Modernization - Banking (BFSI) 
 
How a mid-size private bank can modernize its core banking system without disrupting 
operations. 
Introduction 
A mid-size private bank is running its core operations on a 20 year old mainframe system 
that is expensive to maintain and hard to connect with modern digital channels. Slow 
transaction processing, downtime during batch jobs, and the rising cost of legacy-skilled 
developers are creating serious business and technology challenges. This case study explains 
how the bank can modernize the system through a phased migration strategy, a modern 
technology stack, and strong risk controls.  
Background 
Core banking systems support accounts, payments, loans, and customer records. When these 
systems become outdated, banks struggle to launch digital services quickly and face higher 
maintenance costs. For this bank, modernization is necessary to improve agility, customer 
experience, and long-term efficiency.  
Modernization Strategy 
• Phased Migration - The bank should avoid a full replacement in one go and instead 
modernize module by module, starting with low-risk areas such as reporting, 
notifications, and customer onboarding.  
• API Layer - An API layer should connect the old core with mobile apps, internet 
banking, and third-party systems so digital services can improve without changing 
the full mainframe immediately.  
• Strangler Approach - New services can gradually replace old ones over time, 
reducing risk and allowing live banking operations to continue.  
• Wave-Based Data Migration - Active customer and transaction data should move 
first, while older records can be migrated later in stages.  
Technology Stack 
The proposed stack should include hybrid cloud infrastructure, microservices, API 
management, container platforms, modern databases, and DevSecOps tools. This 
architecture improves scalability, speeds up development, and supports secure integration 
across banking channels.  
Risk Mitigation Plan 
• Parallel Run - Run both legacy and modern systems together before final cutover.  
• Pilot Launch - Start with a limited product, branch group, or customer segment.  
• Testing and Rollback - Use strong testing at every stage and keep rollback plans 
ready.  
• Compliance and Training - Ensure regulatory compliance and train staff to work 
smoothly with the new system.  
 
 
Impact 
This modernization can lead to faster transaction processing, lower downtime, better digital 
integration, and reduced long-term maintenance costs. It also helps the bank launch new 
services faster and reduce dependence on outdated technology and scarce legacy talent.  
Final Note 
Legacy modernization in banking should be treated as a business transformation, not just a 
technical migration. A phased approach with APIs, microservices, and careful risk 
management is the most practical way for a mid-size private bank to modernize without 
disrupting live operations.  
Questions for Discussion 
• Why is phased migration better than a full replacement for banks?  
• How does the strangler approach reduce operational risk?  
• What role does an API layer play in legacy modernization?  
• How can banks balance modernization with regulatory compliance?

title: Customer Support Automation
question:
• How can AI chatbots reduce routine call center volume in telecom? 
• What role does self-service play in improving customer satisfaction?  
• How can automation reduce agent attrition in repetitive support environments?  
• What should remain human-led even after customer support automation?
solution_approach:
Customer Support Automation 
 
How a telecom operator can reduce call center cost while maintaining customer 
satisfaction. 
Introduction 
A telecom operator with around 15 million subscribers is seeing call center volumes grow 20 
percent year over year, mainly due to routine queries such as bill disputes, plan upgrades, and 
balance checks. Long wait times, high agent attrition, and rising cost per call are affecting 
both service quality and profitability. This case study explains what technology and process 
interventions the company can adopt to reduce call volume and cost while maintaining 
customer satisfaction.  
Background 
Telecom companies handle a very large number of customer interactions every day.When a 
large share of these calls is related to simple and repetitive issues, call centers become 
overloaded and agents spend less time on complex customer problems. For a telecom operator 
of this size, automation is necessary not only to control costs but also to improve speed, 
convenience, and consistency in customer service.  
Automation Strategies 
• AI Chatbots and Virtual Assistants - The company should deploy AI-powered 
chatbots on its app, website, and messaging channels to handle common requests such 
as balance checks, bill explanations, recharge support, and plan recommendations.  
• Interactive Voice Response Optimization - A smarter IVR system can identify 
customer intent quickly and offer self-service options before routing calls to agents.  
• Self-Service Portal - A simple digital self-service portal can allow users to resolve 
common problems on their own, such as changing plans, downloading bills, raising 
service requests, and checking usage.  
• Process Automation - Robotic process automation can be used in the backend to 
speed up repetitive tasks such as ticket creation, verification, and complaint routing.  
• Agent Assist Tools - For calls that still reach human agents, AI tools can provide 
suggested responses, next-best actions, and real-time customer information to reduce 
handling time.  
Process Improvements 
Along with technology, the operator should redesign customer support processes. It should 
classify call reasons, identify the top repeat issues, simplify billing communication, and 
improve first-contact resolution. Customer education through app notifications, FAQs, and 
SMS guidance can also reduce avoidable inbound calls.  
Impact 
These interventions can create several positive outcomes: 
• Lower Call Volume - Routine queries shift to digital and automated channels.  
 
• Reduced Cost per Call - Fewer manual interactions lower staffing and operating 
costs.  
• Better Customer Experience - Faster resolution and shorter wait times improve 
satisfaction.  
• Lower Agent Attrition - Agents spend less time on repetitive issues and more on 
meaningful customer support.  
• Higher Scalability - The operator can manage growth without expanding the call 
center at the same pace.  
Final Note 
Customer support automation should not aim to remove human interaction completely. 
Instead, it should automate repetitive queries and allow human agents to focus on high-value 
and emotionally sensitive cases. A balanced model combining AI, self-service, process 
improvement, and assisted support is the most practical way for a telecom operator to reduce 
cost while maintaining customer satisfaction.  
Questions for Discussion 
• How can AI chatbots reduce routine call center volume in telecom? 
• What role does self-service play in improving customer satisfaction?  
• How can automation reduce agent attrition in repetitive support environments?  
• What should remain human-led even after customer support automation?

title: Cloud Migration – Retail/E–commerce
question:
• Why is auto-scaling important for e-commerce platforms? 
• How do microservices improve scalability? 
• What role does a CDN play during festive traffic spikes? 
• Why is phased migration safer than a big-bang move to the cloud?
solution_approach:
Cloud Migration - Retail/E-commerce 
 
How a retail chain can redesign its e-commerce platform to handle traffic spikes. 
Introduction 
A retail chain’s e-commerce platform, hosted on-premise, has faced repeated crashes during 
festive sales and flash discounts. The current infrastructure cannot auto-scale, causing lost 
sales, poor customer experience, and reputational damage during peak traffic events. This 
case study explains how the company can redesign its cloud architecture and migration plan 
to handle unpredictable demand. 
Background 
Retail e-commerce platforms see sudden traffic spikes during campaigns, holidays, and 
discount events. If the system runs on fixed on-premise infrastructure, it cannot expand 
quickly enough when demand surges. For this company, cloud migration is needed to improve 
scalability, reliability, and performance without interrupting operations. 
Migration Strategy 
• Lift and Shift - Move the current platform to cloud infrastructure first to gain 
flexibility quickly. 
• Microservices Architecture - Split key functions such as browsing, cart, checkout, 
and payments into independent services. 
• Containerization - Use containers so services can be deployed and scaled 
independently. 
• Auto-Scaling - Add cloud auto-scaling and load balancing to increase capacity during 
sudden traffic spikes. 
• CDN and Caching - Use a content delivery network and caching layers to speed up 
static content and reduce load on the core system. 
Scaling Design 
The redesigned platform should run on a cloud or hybrid-cloud setup with high availability 
across multiple zones. Databases should be tuned for peak traffic, and monitoring tools should 
track performance, errors, and utilization in real time. This allows the business to scale before 
outages affect customers. 
Risk Mitigation 
• Phased Migration - Move the system in stages rather than all at once. 
• Parallel Run - Keep the old and new environments active during transition. 
• Stress Testing - Simulate festive-sale traffic before major events. 
• Rollback Plan - Prepare fallback options if cutover fails. 
• Security Controls - Protect customer, payment, and transaction data with encryption 
and access control. 
 
 
Impact 
This redesign can reduce downtime, improve site speed, and protect revenue during peak 
campaigns. It also improves customer trust because the site remains stable during sudden 
demand spikes. Over time, the company can pay for capacity more efficiently instead of 
overbuilding fixed infrastructure. 
Final Note 
The best approach is a phased cloud migration supported by microservices, auto-scaling, 
CDN delivery, and strong monitoring. That combination gives the retailer a resilient platform 
that can handle traffic spikes and protect sales. 
Questions for Discussion 
• Why is auto-scaling important for e-commerce platforms? 
• How do microservices improve scalability? 
• What role does a CDN play during festive traffic spikes? 
• Why is phased migration safer than a big-bang move to the cloud?

static content and reduce load on the core system. 
Scaling Design 
The redesigned platform should run on a cloud or hybrid-cloud setup with high availability 
across multiple zones. Databases should be tuned for peak traffic, and monitoring tools should 
track performance, errors, and utilization in real time. This allows the business to scale before 
outages affect customers. 
Risk Mitigation 
• Phased Migration - Move the system in stages rather than all at once. 
• Parallel Run - Keep the old and new environments active during transition. 
• Stress Testing - Simulate festive-sale traffic before major events. 
• Rollback Plan - Prepare fallback options if cutover fails. 
• Security Controls - Protect customer, payment, and transaction data with encryption 
and access control. 
 
 
Impact 
This redesign can reduce downtime, improve site speed, and protect revenue during peak 
campaigns. It also improves customer trust because the site remains stable during sudden 
demand spikes. Over time, the company can pay for capacity more efficiently instead of 
overbuilding fixed infrastructure. 
Final Note 
The best approach is a phased cloud migration supported by microservices, auto-scaling, 
CDN delivery, and strong monitoring. That combination gives the retailer a resilient platform 
that can handle traffic spikes and protect sales. 
Questions for Discussion 
• Why is auto-scaling important for e-commerce platforms? 
• How do microservices improve scalability? 
• What role does a CDN play during festive traffic spikes? 
• Why is phased migration safer than a big-bang move to the cloud?

title: Cybersecurity Overhaul – Healthcare
question:
• Why is zero trust important in healthcare cybersecurity? 
• How does encryption protect patient records? 
• What role does real-time monitoring play in ransomware defense? 
• How can hospitals align cybersecurity controls with HIPAA and GDPR?
solution_approach:
Cybersecurity Overhaul - Healthcare 
 
How a hospital network can secure patient data and achieve compliance after a 
ransomware attack. 
Introduction 
A hospital network managing electronic health records for over 500,000 patients has suffered 
a ransomware attack exposing sensitive patient data. Outdated security infrastructure, no 
encryption on stored data, no real-time threat monitoring, and non-compliance with 
HIPAA/GDPR are putting the organization at risk of fines and loss of trust. This case study 
explains the security architecture and remediation roadmap needed to prevent future breaches 
and restore compliance. 
Background 
Healthcare organizations are frequent targets for cyberattacks because they store highly 
sensitive patient records. When data is not encrypted and threats are not detected in real time, 
attackers can move quickly and damage both operations and trust. For this hospital network, 
cybersecurity is a patient safety, compliance, and business continuity issue. 
Security Architecture 
• Zero Trust Model - Verify every user and device before granting access. 
• Encryption - Encrypt patient records at rest and in transit. 
• IAM and MFA - Use role-based access control, least privilege, and multi-factor 
authentication. 
• Real-Time Monitoring - Deploy SIEM and endpoint detection to spot suspicious 
activity early. 
• Network Segmentation - Separate critical systems to limit the spread of an attack. 
Remediation Roadmap 
• Containment - Isolate affected systems and compromised accounts. 
• Recovery - Restore from clean backups and verify system integrity. 
• Hardening - Patch vulnerabilities and update legacy security controls. 
• Compliance - Align policies and controls with HIPAA and GDPR requirements. 
• Training - Conduct regular awareness training and incident-response drills. 
Impact 
This approach can reduce breach risk, improve detection speed, protect patient trust, and 
strengthen regulatory readiness. It also helps the hospital build a more resilient security 
posture over time. 
Final Note 
A healthcare cybersecurity overhaul should combine prevention, detection, response, and 
compliance in one plan. The best strategy is a phased transformation built around zero trust, 
encryption, continuous monitoring, and strong governance. 
 
Questions for Discussion 
• Why is zero trust important in healthcare cybersecurity? 
• How does encryption protect patient records? 
• What role does real-time monitoring play in ransomware defense? 
• How can hospitals align cybersecurity controls with HIPAA and GDPR?

title: IT Helpdesk Outsourcing – Manufacturing
question:
• Why should only L1 support be outsourced in this model? 
• How does a self-service portal reduce helpdesk load? 
• What should remain under internal IT control in a manufacturing setup? 
• How can SLAs protect support quality after outsourcing?
solution_approach:
IT Helpdesk Outsourcing - Manufacturing 
 
How a large manufacturing firm can free its internal IT team for strategic projects. 
Introduction 
A large manufacturing firm is spending nearly 70% of its internal IT team’s time on routine 
L1 and L2 tickets. As a result, strategic projects like ERP upgrades and factory digitization 
are getting delayed because the team does not have enough bandwidth. 
Background 
Manufacturing companies rely on IT not only for office systems but also for production 
support, shop-floor connectivity, and enterprise applications. When the internal team spends 
most of its time on repetitive helpdesk work, it has less capacity for transformation and 
business-critical improvements. 
Support Delivery Model 
• Outsource L1 Support - Routine password resets, access issues, and basic 
troubleshooting should be handled by an external helpdesk partner. 
• Keep L2/L3 Internal - Complex incidents, plant-critical systems, and architecture 
decisions should remain with the internal team. 
• Self-Service Portal - A portal and knowledge base can solve many repetitive issues 
without human intervention. 
• Standard Ticket Routing - Tickets should be classified clearly so that each issue 
goes to the right support level quickly. 
• SLA-Based Governance - The vendor should be managed through service-level 
agreements, escalation rules, and monthly reviews. 
Operating Improvements 
The firm should identify the most common tickets, automate repeat tasks, and document 
solutions in a shared knowledge base. It should also define which systems are business-
critical so that factory operations are never exposed to poor issue handling or slow escalation. 
Impact 
This model can reduce the workload on the internal IT team, improve ticket resolution 
efficiency, and allow faster progress on ERP and digital transformation projects. It also 
improves scalability because the outsourcing layer can absorb high volumes of routine 
requests while internal staff focus on strategic work. 
Final Note 
The best approach is not full outsourcing, but a hybrid model that keeps strategic control 
inside while shifting repetitive work outside. That balance helps the manufacturing firm 
protect operations, improve support quality, and free its internal team for transformation 
work. 
 
 
Questions for Discussion 
• Why should only L1 support be outsourced in this model? 
• How does a self-service portal reduce helpdesk load? 
• What should remain under internal IT control in a manufacturing setup? 
• How can SLAs protect support quality after outsourcing?

title: Network Infrastructure Upgrade
question:
• Why is network virtualization important for telecom modernization? 
• How does edge computing help in dense urban areas? 
• What makes SDN useful for congestion management? 
• Why should 5G upgrades be done in phases?
solution_approach:
Network Infrastructure Upgrade 
 
How a regional telecom provider can reduce congestion and prepare for 5G. 
Introduction 
A regional telecom provider is facing network congestion in dense urban areas, resulting in 
dropped calls and inconsistent data speeds. Its legacy hardware-based network architecture 
is rigid, expensive to scale, and not ready for the upcoming 5G rollout. 
Background 
Telecom networks in cities carry high traffic from voice, data, and streaming usage. When 
infrastructure depends on fixed hardware, it becomes difficult to expand capacity quickly or 
reroute traffic efficiently during peak load periods. For this provider, modernization is 
necessary to improve service quality, reduce congestion, and support next-generation 
connectivity. 
Architectural Changes 
• Virtualized Network Functions - Shift from fixed hardware appliances to software-
based network functions that can scale more easily. 
• SDN Architecture - Use software-defined networking to manage traffic dynamically 
and improve routing efficiency. 
• Edge Computing - Place compute closer to users in dense urban areas to reduce 
latency and improve speed. 
• 5G-Ready Core - Upgrade the core network to support 5G standards, higher 
bandwidth, and lower-latency services. 
• Load Balancing and Monitoring - Use traffic balancing, real-time monitoring, and 
predictive analytics to manage congestion before service quality drops. 
These changes move the network from a rigid hardware model to a flexible, software-led 
design. That makes it easier to manage urban traffic spikes and prepare for higher demand. 
Rollout Plan 
The provider should modernize the network in phases, starting with the most congested city 
zones. Pilot deployments, performance testing, and fallback planning are important so that 
critical services remain stable during the transition. Security, vendor coordination, and 
service continuity should remain central throughout the migration. 
Impact 
This upgrade can reduce dropped calls, improve data speeds, lower scaling costs, and 
increase network resilience. It also creates a stronger foundation for 5G services and future 
digital offerings. Over time, the provider can handle urban traffic growth without depending 
on rigid legacy systems. 
 
 
 
Final Note 
The best approach is a phased shift toward software-defined, virtualized, and edge-enabled 
infrastructure. That combination gives the telecom provider better reliability today and a 
practical path to 5G readiness. 
Questions for Discussion 
• Why is network virtualization important for telecom modernization? 
• How does edge computing help in dense urban areas? 
• What makes SDN useful for congestion management? 
• Why should 5G upgrades be done in phases?

title: Case 1: The Ad That Didn't Match the Brand
question:
Case 1: The Ad That Didn't Match the Brand
Domain: Sales and Marketing  |  Decision Archetype: Positioning Strategy  |  Framework: STP +
Positioning Map
Mumbai, a Tuesday morning.
Rhea Malhotra, CMO of NovaTel, was scrolling through her phone when her sister forwarded a
WhatsApp message: "Since when did NovaTel become this fancy? Thought you guys were for
students and small shopkeepers?"
Attached was NovaTel's new ad — sleek visuals, a Bollywood actor in a blazer, the tagline:
"NovaTel. For Those Who Lead."
NovaTel had built its base over six years as the go-to network for tier-2 towns, college students,
and small business owners — cheap recharges, simple plans, no frills. Last quarter, the leadership
team decided the brand needed to "move up" to compete with premium players chasing urban
professionals. They hired a new agency, repositioned the brand as aspirational, and rolled out the
campaign nationally.
Three weeks in, the numbers were confusing. Urban sign-ups had barely moved. But in NovaTel's
original strongholds — the small towns — recharge renewals had dropped 12%. Customer care
was flooded with messages like Rhea's sister's: confusion, mild betrayal, jokes about NovaTel
"getting too big for its boots."
Rhea called a meeting with the research team. They pulled together two simple pieces of data: a
customer perception survey (asking existing users to rate NovaTel and three rivals on "Affordable
to Premium" and "Basic to Trustworthy") and a quick breakdown of who was actually renewing
plans versus dropping off.
The perception map was clear: NovaTel's original loyal base saw the brand as affordable and
trustworthy — not premium, not aspirational. The new campaign hadn't shifted urban perception
much yet, but it had already confused the core base.
Rhea had two weeks before the board reviewed campaign performance. She had to decide: push
forward and give the repositioning more time, walk it back to the old identity, or find some middle
ground that kept both audiences happy.
Exhibit 1 — Perception Map
Customers plotted NovaTel and 3 rivals on two axes (Affordable↔Premium, Basic↔Trustworthy).
NovaTel sits firmly in the affordable-trustworthy quadrant; competitors are spread across premium
quadrants.
Exhibit 2 — Renewal Data by City Tier

Campaign)

Campaign)

Tier 2/3 (Core base)

Discussion Questions
1. Should NovaTel continue the premium repositioning, or reverse it?
2. Can a brand serve both its loyal base and a new aspirational audience at the same time?
3. If you were Rhea, what would you tell the board in two weeks?
Digital & Telecom Casebook — 12 Short Strategy Cases
solution_approach:
NovaTel case, solved
Sales & Marketing case study  |  Framework: STP + Positioning map
The framework, in plain words
STP means Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning. First you split customers into groups. Then you pick the
group you want to win. Then you decide the one clear promise you make to that group. A positioning map is just
a picture that checks if your promise matches what customers already believe about you.
Where NovaTel really stands
Customers already see NovaTel as affordable and trustworthy, a space no rival owns. The new ad is pulling NovaTel toward
premium, straight into a corner where three rivals already live. That is a hard fight to win, and it puts NovaTel's safest space
at risk.
What happened to renewals

Urban renewals barely moved, up just 2 points. But the loyal core base dropped 12 points in three weeks. The campaign is
already costing more than it has gained anywhere.
Q1. Push on, or reverse the campaign?
Neither. A full reversal wastes the money already spent and looks like panic. But running the same campaign
everywhere for months would let the bleeding continue. The fix is to pause the campaign in tier-2 and tier-3
towns right away, since it was never meant for them, and keep testing it only in big cities.
Q2. Can one brand serve both groups?
Yes, but not with one single message. Airlines do this well: budget seats and business class sit under one
airline, but they never mix their messaging. NovaTel can keep its main brand affordable and trustworthy for its
loyal base, and launch a separate premium name, like “NovaTel Prime,” for city professionals. Two audiences,
two promises, one company.
Q3. What should Rhea tell the board?
Lead with the data, not the anecdote. Show the positioning map: NovaTel is repositioning into a crowded space
while giving up an empty one. Show the renewal drop: real cost, no gain yet. Recommend pausing the
campaign in core towns immediately, and testing a separate premium sub-brand in cities for one more quarter,
with renewal numbers tracked by tier this time.
The one-line takeaway
This was not a failed repositioning. It was an unsegmented one. Fix the targeting, keep the ambition.
